There is also a very subtle connection among the sentences of this paragraph, just as we explained in the sentences of the previous paragraph.

﴿He has ordained for you of the religion that which He enjoined upon Nuh, and that which We have revealed to you (O Muhammad ﷺ), and that which We enjoined upon Ibrahim, Musa and Isa, (saying): Establish the religion and do not be divided therein.﴾ (42:13) By this, the reality is made clear, the details of which we gave at the beginning of the surah: the roots of the religions are one. In terms of time and place, it has developed in different eras. From this, a believer may have such thoughts and feelings that he considers his past to be very long, his predecessors to be very great people, and himself to be a follower and adherent of such great people: Nuh (peace be upon him), Ibrahim (peace be upon him), Musa (peace be upon him), Isa (peace be upon him), Muhammad (ﷺ). This awareness becomes firm: that this religion is a continuation of the earlier religions, and that it proceeds on the path of the prophets and messengers. And on this path it moves with great joy, even though there may be fatigue and difficulties, and he may have to sacrifice many of his worldly interests. The believer attains the firm awareness that he is a member of the caravan of great people, and that this caravan is the caravan of great people throughout the whole of human history.

That those who follow this religion of Allah have lasting peace and harmony among themselves. They stand on one permanent Shariah and one highway. There is no disagreement or enmity among them; rather, there are deep ties and connections among them. These ties and connections demand further mutual bonding and reconciliation. Thus the present state of the believers becomes linked with their past, and their past becomes joined with their present, and they all set out on one and the same path.

If the Islamic system and Shariah that Allah has prescribed for the believers and the Muslims is the same as that which was enjoined and emphasised upon Nuh, Ibrahim, Musa and Isa, peace be upon them, before it, then why do the followers of Musa and Isa (peace be upon them) fight and quarrel with one another? Then why are different sects among the followers of Isa (peace be upon him) at each other's throats? Then why do the followers of Musa and Isa (peace be upon them) harbour enmity towards the followers of Muhammad (ﷺ)? Then, what is the answer for those who claim that they follow the religion of Ibrahim, namely the polytheists of Arabia? Why are they the enemies of Muhammad (ﷺ), and why do they not gather under the banner of the Final Prophet, whose call is that all his followers should follow one religion? It was enjoined upon them that: ﴿Establish the religion and do not be divided therein.﴾ (42:13) Why do they not fulfil their duties? Why do they not give up deviation, repent from crookedness, and why do they not stand in one solid row under the banner of the last Prophet? Because after Nuh, Ibrahim, Musa and Isa (peace be upon them), now it is the turn of Muhammad (ﷺ), and this trust has now come to him.

﴿It is hard for the polytheists, that to which you call them.﴾ (42:13) This matter is grievous to these polytheists: that among them, revelation should come down upon Muhammad, son of Abdullah. Whereas their thinking was that this revelation would descend upon some great man of the two towns.

﴿Upon a great man of the two towns﴾ (43:31), that is, that it would be revealed upon one of the great men and rulers of those two villages. But even their claim was not correct as a matter of fact: Muhammad (ﷺ), according to their own statement, was truthful and trustworthy, and he was a son of an outstanding clan of the Quraysh. He was indeed a great man.

This new call was hard for them, because if it succeeds, the era of idol worship will end, idols and the myths about idols will come to an end, and on this their leadership and authority were founded. Their personal and economic interests were tied to these notions. Therefore they embraced polytheism, and pure monotheism, which the messengers called to, weighed heavily upon them.

Furthermore, it was also grievous to them that their forefathers who had died in ignorance had died in misguidance, and that they were disbelievers and people of Hell. So they said: if our forefathers are people of Hell, then we are too. Thus they became stubborn, and out of a wrong path of hostility they took hold of it, and they deliberately prepared to throw themselves into Hell, only because they were not willing to declare their forefathers to be misguided.

The Holy Qur'an refutes their position that it is Allah's right to choose whomever He wills. In this way Allah turns His attention only to those who wish to come under His protection, and He returns those rejected people through repentance:

﴿Allah chooses for Himself whom He wills, and guides to Himself whoever turns (to Him) penitently.﴾ (42:13) So Allah chose Muhammad (ﷺ). And whoever now turns towards the path shown by Allah, Allah will guide him.

Now the address turns back to the position of the followers of the great prophets mentioned above, whom Allah sent with one religion, and who presented one religion to their people, but whose followers introduced divisions into it:

﴿And they did not become divided except after knowledge had come to them, out of envy among themselves. And if not for a word that had preceded from your Lord (to delay) until a specified term, the matter would have been judged between them. And indeed, those who were given the Scripture after them are in grave doubt concerning it.﴾ (42:14) The divisions that arose among the people occurred after knowledge had come to them, and they occurred because they wanted to oppress one another. If your Lord had not already decreed that the decision would be deferred to a fixed time, their dispute would have been settled. The truth is that those who were made heirs of the Scripture after the earlier ones are in a disquieting doubt about it. In the first place, these differences were not due to ignorance. It was not because they did not know the real truth, or did not know the source of the teaching of the messengers; rather, they doubted it while knowing it well. They divided because of mutual enmity. These disputes arose because of malice and jealousy. Cruel desires compelled them to divide, and uncontrollable desires of the self forced them. This division did not occur because they had no proof for correct beliefs, or because they had no evidence from the way of life that was given to them. If they had remained sincerely firm on their true belief and Shariah, they would not have divided.

These people deserved that Allah should seize them, and that His punishment should come upon them swiftly, because of their rebelliousness and their injustice, which they did to the true religion by dividing it. But Allah, in the arrangement of the universe, had already made a decision beforehand, and a respite was granted to them until a fixed time.

﴿And if not for a word that had preceded from your Lord (to delay) until a specified term, the matter would have been judged between them.﴾ (42:14) In this way, in these differences, truth would have become truth and falsehood would have become falsehood, and the matter would have been concluded in this worldly life itself. But they were granted respite until a known time.

Those generations which became the heirs of the earlier followers who had divided, and to whom this Book came, did not receive this Book and this doctrine with certainty. Because the record of their disagreements was before them, and nothing definite and conclusive emerged from it. All the sectarian differences were confused, unclear and distressing.

﴿And indeed, those who were given the Scripture after them are in grave doubt concerning it.﴾ (42:14) Thus belief is like a firm rock around which the earth moves, yet it stands firm. A believer firmly settles upon that solid rock, and no earthquake can remove him from his place. Belief is like a star that stays fixed in its place, and despite waves and storms, the believer's eye is upon his star on the far horizon, which determines the direction. In this way a believer does not lose his way, even if he is in dark seas. But when belief and doctrine themselves become doubtful, then no one's word can remain stable. If they themselves are in agitation and doubt, they cannot lead anyone. "Who can awaken a sleeper but another sleeper?" "The reality is that the leaders of the other major religions have become prey in the hands of players and gamblers, and they are under the influence of distorters and hypocrites. These religions have lost their spirit and their form. If Allah were to bring back to life the first adherents of these religions, they would not be able to recognise those religions that are attributed to their own names. Thus, while at one time these religions were givers of civilisation, culture, government and politics, now from them come disorder, corruption, differences and anarchy. Rulers are wicked in their deeds, lost in their own selves. They have no message for nations or for the world. In terms of lofty aims they are bankrupt. The springs of their lives have dried up; in the light of heavenly guidance they have no path, nor do they have any stable and firm way of life."

The famous American author George H. Danson, in his book *Emotion as the Basis of Civilization*, writes:

"In the fifth and sixth centuries of the Christian era, the world of religion was on the brink of a deep pit of destruction. Because the ideas that had helped to give birth to civilisation had come to an end, and there was no doctrine present to take the place of the religions of that time. And it was becoming clearly visible that the human civilisation which had taken four thousand years to build and develop was about to be destroyed and ruined, and humanity was about to be trapped again in ignorance and the tribal system, in which there is no law or order, because the collective order and administration that Christianity had established was about to collapse. For Christianity had become divided into sects; it had no unity and no order within it. In that period, civilisation was like a great tree whose branches spread and whose shade covered the whole world. This tree stood in a state of great weakness in the face of severe storms, and destruction was knocking at its door, when in the midst of this a person (Muhammad ﷺ) was born."

This situation arose because the bearers of the heavenly religions had begun to have severe disagreements among themselves, after knowledge had come to them. And those who became the heirs of the Book after the first people of the religions were in doubt about the truth of those very books. Because of these causes, and because of the disappearance of a centre to lead humanity throughout the world, Muhammad (ﷺ) was sent, and he was commanded to walk upon the straight path, to call people to it, and to let people say whatever they wished about his clear and manifest doctrines and his firm call. He should not turn his attention to anyone, and he should declare that this call and this system are the same that Allah gave to all the prophets and about which He enjoined them.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on surah 42, verses 13–16 (part 2 of 2):

﴿So, to that end, invite (them), and remain steadfast as you have been commanded, and do not follow their desires, and say: "I believe in whatever Book Allah has sent down, and I have been commanded to act justly among you. Allah is our Lord and your Lord. For us are our deeds and for you are your deeds. There is no argument between us and you. Allah will gather us all together, and to Him is the final return."﴾ (42:15)

Now the Islamic call was, as it were, a new leadership for all of humanity. It was a wise and rightly-guided leadership, whose system of life was clear and which possessed firm conviction. It called to Allah, worked with insight (ʿala wajh al-basirah) toward its goal, and proceeded on the command of God without any deviation. It did not follow changing aims and changing desires in its decisions. It was a leadership whose message was one, whose Book was one, whose system of law was one, and whose faith was traced back to its source of faith. And it had returned all of humanity to one important principle.

﴿And say: "I believe in whatever Book Allah has sent down."﴾ (42:15) After this, this call, this movement, rises in the world carrying the truth of the call and attains sovereign authority, so that it may act justly among people.

﴿I have been commanded to act justly among you.﴾ (42:15) This is a leadership that has authority and that proclaims justice on the earth. (The Prophet ﷺ is saying this at a time when the Islamic call is in Makkah and the caller and the movement are besieged in the Shi'b Abi Talib, and mountains of calamities are being heaped upon them; yet even there the temperament of the Islamic call, its dominant temperament, is entirely clear) (Translator). This call proclaims that the Lord is one.

﴿Allah is our Lord and your Lord.﴾ (42:15) It also proclaims that every person is responsible for his own deeds and that the accountability is individual.

﴿For us are our deeds and for you are your deeds.﴾ (42:15) Therefore, idle debate and argument should now come to an end.

﴿There is no argument between us and you.﴾ (42:15)

﴿Allah will gather us together, and to Him is the final return.﴾ (42:15)

This is one verse, yet it fully clarifies the temperament of the Islamic call. Its phrases are short, but they speak in a very plain and decisive manner. This is a call that must remain steadfast on its path and pay no regard to human desires. It must be pure in its sovereign authority over this earth so that it can act justly. It must show all humanity a straight path, which is the right path (sirat mustaqim), and this has been the path of all the messengers.

Therefore, after clarifying the Islamic call in this manner, and after a group of the believers has responded to this call, there is no longer any opportunity to give heed to the words of those who quarrel and engage in useless disputation. All their arguments have been nullified; they carry no weight and have no significance. Therefore a decisive word is now spoken concerning them, and they are left to face the severe threat of Allah.

﴿And those who dispute concerning Allah after it has been responded to, their argument is baseless in the sight of their Lord, and upon them is wrath, and for them is a severe punishment.﴾ (42:16) After the call of Allah has been answered, those who dispute about Allah's matter, their argument is baseless in the sight of their Lord, and upon them is His wrath, and for them is a severe punishment. Those who dispute concerning Allah, and whose argument is baseless in the sight of Allah, then their dispute is baseless and their proof has no standing. Their argument is rejected on earth too, and in the Hereafter they will face the severe wrath and punishment of Allah. This idle quarrel and argumentation is an appropriate punishment for them, especially when they see that the most sincere and wise people have accepted this call. Therefore, their discussion and debate come after the truth has been made clear, and they are for other purposes.

Now the direction of the discourse turns again to the original subject.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 42, verses 17–20:

Verses 17 to 19

Allah sent down the Book with truth, and within it He sent down the balance (mizan) of justice. In accordance with this balance, He commanded that people's disputes be judged and decided. Whether the matter concerns people's desires and claims, their opinions, or their beliefs and ideologies, the judgment is to be made by it. Allah also sent down a system of Shari'ah (divine law) founded upon just decisions. The Qur'an uses the word mizan for justice, meaning a justice by which rights can be weighed, and actions and dealings can be measured.

Now the direction of speech moves from the Book and the balance to the Hour (qiyamah). The connection of the theme is clear: the Book and the Shari'ah have to establish justice among people by applying the balance in this world, and justice and fairness will be done by the balance in the Hereafter as well. Since the Hour of Resurrection is an unseen matter, and no one knows the moment of its establishment, it may be very near.

﴿And what will make you know? Perhaps the Hour is near.﴾ (42:17) And people may be heedless of it while it is close to them. And this final balance of justice and fairness will be granted, where no deed will be left in vain and no one will be lost. Here the thinking of both believers and deniers about the Resurrection is described.

﴿Those who do not believe in it seek to hasten it, while those who believe fear it and know that it is the truth.﴾ (42:18) It is evident that those who do not believe in it have no fear of it in their hearts, and they have no idea of what will befall them there. Therefore, in a spirit of mockery, they demand its coming, or demand that it be brought. Because they are blind and do not see it. As for those who are believers, they believe in the Resurrection too. That is why they fear it, and await it with great awe and dread. They know that when it comes, what will happen will be true; its coming is the truth, and the believer recognises it, because there is a bond between the believer and the truth.

﴿Surely those who dispute concerning the Hour are in far-off error.﴾ (42:18) They have gone to extremes in error and have strayed far along this path; now, having gone so far, it is no longer possible for them to return. Now, from the theme of the Hereafter, its denial, heedlessness towards it, and fear of it, the direction of speech turns to the discussion of the provision (rizq) of people in this world, which Allah gives to some in less and to some in more.

﴿Allah is Gentle with His servants; He provides for whom He wills, and He is the Strong, the Mighty.﴾ (42:19) Apparently, there seems to be no particular connection between the themes of the Hereafter and the provision of the servants. But after reading the next verse, the connection becomes apparent.

﴿Whoever desires the tilth of the Hereafter, We increase for him in his tilth; and whoever desires the tilth of this world, We give him of it, but he has no share in the Hereafter.﴾ (42:20) So Allah is very gentle with His servants; He gives to whom He wills. He gives to the righteous and also to the wicked, to the believer and also to the disbeliever, because human beings cannot make provision for their own sustenance on their own. When Allah has given them life, He has also given them the basic means of life. If Allah did not provide for the disbeliever, the sinner and the evildoer, they could not arrange their own sustenance, and they would die of hunger and thirst. When they had lost life itself, the law that Allah established, of granting respite by keeping them alive, would not be fulfilled; and it would not be possible for people to act freely in this world and for their deeds to be reckoned in the Hereafter. Therefore Allah has placed the matter of provision outside the sphere of good and evil. Provision has no connection with faith or disbelief. He placed the matter of provision upon the conditions of human collective life, then upon the conduct of His servants within those collective conditions, and made wealth a trial and test for people, upon which reward and punishment depend.

Then He set separate fields, one for the Hereafter and one for this world. He gave each person the choice of whether to labour in the field of this world or in the field of the Hereafter. Whoever works the field of the Hereafter will receive the harvest of the Hereafter, and Allah, as a reward, will increase his field and, because of his intention, will provide the means for that work and bless it. In this tilth of the Hereafter, his worldly needs will also be provided for: he will receive his worldly provision too, and there will be no shortfall in it. Indeed, this worldly provision itself becomes his success in the Hereafter, when he spends it in the way of Allah and uses it in accordance with Allah's command, by spending in the cause of Allah (infaq fi sabilillah). Whoever desires only the field of this world, Allah gives him the goods of this world, and he receives what has been written for him; but he has no share in the Hereafter, because he never worked in the field of the Hereafter so that anything awaited him there.

Now, if we cast a glance at those who seek the fields of this world and those who seek the fields of the Hereafter, it becomes clear that those who labour only in the field of this world are very foolish. As far as worldly provision is concerned, Allah gives it to both parties, because every person receives sustenance to live in this world according to what is written for him. Yet for the one who labours in the field of the Hereafter, his share of the Hereafter is his alone.

Among those who choose only the field of this world there are both the poor and the wealthy, according to how much wealth each has, in keeping with the general conditions of the society in which he lives, and his own ability and effort. The same is the case among those who labour in the field of the Hereafter: there will be both wealthy and poor among them, because in the matter of provision there is no difference between believer and disbeliever. The difference arises only in which field a person chooses: the world alone, or the Hereafter. The fool is the one who abandons the field of the Hereafter, which contains both the provision of this world and the share of the Hereafter. When he abandons the field of the Hereafter, he receives in this world only what has been decreed for him.

In short, the matter will reach its end in accordance with the truth which Allah has sent down in His Book. The principle of truth and justice is that provision be given to all living things, and that the share of the Hereafter belong only to those who worked for the Hereafter; and those who do not work for the Hereafter shall be deprived of it in the Hereafter.

When he abandons the field of the Hereafter, he receives in this world only what has been decreed for him.

In short, the matter will reach its end in accordance with the truth which Allah has sent down in His Book. The principle of truth and justice is that provision be given to all living things, and that the share of the Hereafter belong only to those who worked for the Hereafter; and those who do not work for the Hereafter shall be deprived of it in the Hereafter.

Now, once again, a journey back to the earlier theme, namely Tawhid and Risalah.

This punishment is their situation because of their wrongdoing, and who could be a greater wrongdoer than one who opposes the Shari'ah of Allah and supports the Shari'ah of others besides Allah. For this reason, these wrongdoers are now presented in one of the scenes of the Hereafter. They are frightened and terrified there, and the punishment of Hell is before them. Before this, they neither feared it nor were apprehensive, but rather they mocked it.

Taral-zalimina mushfiqina mimma kasabu wa huwa waqi'un bihim (42:22) "You will see the wrongdoers fearful of what they have earned, while it will befall them." The Qur'an's manner of expression is very remarkable: these people will then be fearful of "what they earned." Their earnings will be like a calamity from which they will be afraid, and this calamity they themselves earned with their own hands. In the world they were very pleased with this achievement of theirs (non-Islamic legislation), but today they are terrified of it, yet wa huwa waqi'un bihim (42:22) "and it is going to befall them."

And the second glimpse of this scene concerns the believers, who feared that Day but today are in peace and security and are very prosperous:

Wallazina amanu ... al-fadlul-kabir (42:22). Dhalika alladhi yubashshiru ... wa 'amilus-salihat (42:23) "In contrast, those who have believed and done righteous deeds will be in gardens of paradise; whatever they wish they will have with their Lord. That is the great bounty. This is what Allah gives glad tidings of to His servants who have believed and done righteous deeds."

The Qur'an's expression here is also extremely pleasant, gentle and soothing. Rawdatul-jannat: gardens of paradise, many paradises and many gardens. "Whatever they wish they will have with their Lord," without any limits or restrictions. "That is the great bounty." "This is what Allah gives glad tidings of to His servants." This present tense "Allah gives glad tidings" is a present and continuous announcement, and it is the fulfilment of the earlier glad tidings. The atmosphere of good news is the most delightful of all; when someone receives a blessing, the giving of glad tidings makes his sense of it even sharper.

After showing this scene of blessings, gentle and delicate, full of grace and kindness, the Prophet (ﷺ) is commanded to tell them that the guidance I present, through which you will receive these blessings and be kept far from Hell, I present only because you are my relatives and I have love for you; this reward is sufficient for me.

Qul la as'alukum ... ghafurun shakur (42:23) "Say, O Prophet, to these people: I do not ask of you any reward for this work. However, out of the love of kinship, I wish that you be saved from Hell. Whoever earns good, We will increase for him good in it. Indeed, Allah is Forgiving and Appreciative."

The meaning I have indicated is this: I do not seek any reward from you, but the love of kinship compels me to this task. The kinship of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) extended to every branch of Quraysh, and he would strive that his relatives come to guidance. Because of this kinship he wished that this good would reach them, and this is the abundant reward for him. In the Qur'an, wherever this manner of expression occurs, after reading it, in my opinion this meaning is clear. A tafsir from Ibn 'Abbas (رضي الله عنه) is also narrated; I quote it here because it is recorded in Sahih al-Bukhari. Bukhari narrated: from Muhammad ibn Bashshar, from Muhammad ibn Ja'far, from Shu'bah, from 'Abd al-Malik ibn Maysarah, from Tawus, and from Ibn 'Abbas (رضي الله عنه), that he was asked about the verse "al-mawaddata fil-qurba" (42:23), and Sa'id ibn Jubayr said, "It means the relatives of Muhammad's family." Ibn 'Abbas (رضي الله عنه) said, "You have been hasty. The reality is that there was no branch of Quraysh in which the Prophet (ﷺ) did not have kinship." Then he said the meaning is: "except that you maintain the kinship that is between me and you."

According to this hadith, the meaning would be: that you, keeping in view my kinship, refrain from harming me, and listen to what I say and adopt a gentle attitude. This would be sufficient reward. Only this reward do I seek from you; I seek nothing beyond it.

The interpretation of Ibn 'Abbas (رضي الله عنه) is easier to grasp than the interpretation of Sa'id ibn Jubayr. But the meaning I have stated above is closer and more beautiful. Allah knows best.

Whatever the meaning, after the scenes of gardens and glad tidings mentioned, Allah says that the Messenger does not ask any reward from you for this work, and it is most unlikely that those who are being guided would ask him for a reward for it. But these are the grace and kindness of Allah: He does not keep a commercial account with His servants, nor does He reckon them with a strict fair reckoning; Allah's reckoning is full of mercy and bounty.

Wa man yaqtarif hasanatan nazid lahu fiha husna (42:23) "Whoever earns good, We will increase for him good in it." Not only is no reward taken for guidance, but further favours are also given. Then forgiveness is granted if there is any error, and in addition Allah shows appreciation.

Inna Allaha ghafurun shakur (42:23) "Indeed, Allah is Forgiving and Appreciative." Allah pardons and also Himself shows appreciation. To whom does He show appreciation? To His servants, for coming onto the right path, although the very ability to come onto the right path was granted by Him. Furthermore, He increases their attributes, purifies them of evil, and then also shows appreciation. What bounties these are! It is not possible for a human being to treat others in such a way. Only thanks can be offered to Allah, and the ability of the heart to respond can be sought.

Now, let the discourse return once more to the Divine revelation!

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 42, verse 24:

Verse No. 24

Here the final objection of the polytheists is taken up. Regarding revelation, this was their last argument concerning their attitude towards it. Before this, after a detailed explanation of the source and origin of revelation, its nature and essence, and its purposes and objectives, this is now their final question.

﴿Or do they say, "He has fabricated a lie against Allah"?﴾ (42:24) And the real reason is that they do not confirm the Quran, because their assumption is that it is not revelation, and that nothing is coming from Allah.

This question is painful, because how could Allah permit such a person to roam about in Allah's dominion, practising deception in Allah's name, and to claim that revelation is coming to him when no revelation is coming to him? Allah is able to set a seal upon the heart of such a person, so that he is unable to say anything at all, and to expose this falsehood through some other means. In this way He would erase it and make the truth clear and evident.

﴿If Allah willed, He could seal your heart.﴾ [And] ﴿He erases falsehood and establishes the truth by His words.﴾ Nothing is hidden from Allah of what enters the heart of Muhammad (ﷺ). If these matters were not from Allah, He would have erased them.

﴿Indeed, He knows what is within the breasts.﴾ (42:24)

Therefore, this is a doubt that has no reality. It is a claim that contradicts Allah's knowledge and is a challenge to Allah's power, and it is contrary to Allah's established way (sunnah jariyah), because Allah establishes the truth on earth and erases falsehood. Therefore, this revelation is true. Hadrat Muhammad (ﷺ) is truthful and trustworthy (al-sadiq wa al-amin), and the objections and accusations that are made are wrong and false. Thus the discussion of revelation ends here for the time being, and a second lesson begins.

Verse 28

This is another manner that makes them aware that in this world Allah's grace and mercy toward His servants takes many forms. Sometimes a severe drought occurs, the rains stop, and people become unable even to provide for the first necessity of life, which is water. The situation reaches the point where they begin to despair. Then Allah sends down rain. Their need is fulfilled, Allah's mercy spreads, and the earth becomes alive and lush green. Seeds begin to sprout, and plants begin to rise. The atmosphere becomes pleasant, and life is seen moving everywhere. Faces brighten, hearts open, hopes grow, and desires are fulfilled. It should be remembered that between despair and the hope of mercy there are only a few moments. Within moments the doors of Allah's mercy are opened. The doors of the heavens are opened by water.

﴿وَهُوَ الْوَلِيُّ الْحَمِيدُ﴾ (42:28) "And He is the Protecting Friend, the Praiseworthy." He is the Helper and Guardian, and in His essence and attributes He is worthy of all praise.

Here the Qur'an has used the word ghayth for rain, which includes the meaning of assistance and succour. Providing help at a time when people are in hardship and calamity is ghayth. Similarly, the result of this help is named mercy.

﴿وَيَنْشُرُ رَحْمَتَهُ﴾ (42:28) "and spreads His mercy." From this come the meanings of freshness, greenery, hope and joy, which appear outwardly in the form of the spreading of mercy through the sprouting of plants and the emergence of fruits. Whenever the rain of mercy descends after a prolonged drought, the joy of people, the refreshment of their bodies and nerves, and the delight of their hearts and minds are a sight to behold. After such a drought, when the earth becomes green with vegetation, all anxieties vanish from human hearts. The dead earth comes back to life.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 42, verses 29–31:

Verses 29 to 31

This sign is constantly before human eyes, and when revelation came, it bore witness to it. They doubted revelation and kept disputing about it, but regarding the sign of the creation of the heavens and the earth, there is no doubt; it is definitive in its indication. It addresses human nature in its natural language. No serious thinker can hold any difference of opinion about it. This sign shows that the Being who created the heavens and the earth is not a human being, nor does any of God's creation appear to be the creator of this sign. Therefore, there is no recourse but to acknowledge a Creator and Governor.

The terrifying vastness of this universe, the subtle and precise uniformity of its motion, the astonishing continuity of its system, and the operation of one law of nature and one order of creation throughout the entire universe: no rational explanation for all these matters can be offered except that there is one Being, the Lord of the worlds (Ilah al-'Alamin), who is managing it. As for human nature, it directly perceives this argument and these signs, and upon comprehending them it becomes satisfied, before ever hearing a single word from any external source.

This great sign of the heavens and the earth contains within it many signs.

"And of His signs is the creation of the heavens and the earth, and whatever living creatures He has scattered throughout them both" (42:29). Leave aside whether there is life in the heavens or not, of which we still have no knowledge; yet the variety of life on this earth is a most magnificent sign. It is a secret such that no one has yet reached its essence. To create it is far beyond anyone's reach. It is a hidden mystery where life comes from and how it comes, and how it becomes joined within bodies. Until today, in all the efforts made to discover the reality of life, all the doors to discovering this secret have been found closed. Whatever has been discovered concerns the development and growth of life after life has existed, the variety of life, and its purposes and wisdoms. Even within this limited scope, there is immense disagreement among opinions and theories. What lies behind apparent life is behind a veil; no eye can see there, and no perceiving power can comprehend it. It is a matter of God's command, and none knows it except God.

This variety of living creatures that is on the surface of the earth, within the surface, in the seas, and in the boundless skies: of these, humans know only a very small portion. As for whether there are other living creatures in this extremely vast universe of unimaginable expanses, we have no information about it. Even of the life present and observable on the surface of the earth, we have been able to know only a very small part. These living creatures that are in the heavens and the earth, Allah will gather them together on the day He wills. Not a single individual who has come into existence since the beginning of the universe will be left behind or be able to remain hidden.

The condition of humans is such that if a flock of birds flies out of their cages, or a swarm of bees flies out of a hive, they cannot gather it back. As for flocks of birds, how many there are, only Allah knows. Then, as for hives of flies, ants, and other similar creatures, Allah alone knows about them too. Only Allah can count them. As for insects, worms, and microbes, only Allah knows their number and their places. As for fish and other sea creatures, only Allah knows their number and kinds. As for the kinds and numbers of domestic and wild animals, where they are scattered, knowledge of this also belongs to Allah alone. And then, as for human settlements, groups, nations, and types, Allah alone is aware of where they have lived, where they live, and where they will live. Besides these kinds, there are countless creations, more in number than these, hidden in the heavens and the earth, and Allah alone knows them as well. They are all Allah's creation. When Allah gathers them, He will gather them in the twinkling of an eye, with a single word. In a single verse, both scenes of the scattering of all these living beings and their gathering are shown, before the sentence is fully uttered from the tongue. The scene appears on the screen of the mind first and then passes. This is the particular style of the Qur'an.

Between these scenes, they are told that because of your deeds, calamities have also come upon you in this world. These calamities are not complete; rather, a part of them comes upon you. Most of the time Allah pardons, because Allah does not punish people with the full measure of their deeds. Allah overlooks many evil deeds. Allah reminds them that you are very helpless and powerless. You cannot prevent any of Allah's plans. You are only a small part of this universe.

"Whatever affliction befalls you is because of what your own hands have earned, and He pardons much" (42:30). "And you cannot escape [Allah] within the earth, and you have not besides Allah any protector or helper" (42:31). In the first verse there is a manifestation of Allah's justice, and upon humanity there are manifestations of Allah's mercy. Whatever afflictions come upon them come because of what their own hands have earned. But Allah Himself, by seizing them, pardons all their wrongdoings, because He knows that man is very weak. His natural inclinations and his environment compel him toward wrongdoing. Therefore Allah pardons many sins. These are His mercies and kindnesses.

In the second verse there is an expression of human weakness: that he cannot prevent any of Allah's plans on the earth. (Likewise, he cannot stop the Islamic call.) He has no guardian or helper except Allah. Therefore, a person should return to his true Guardian.

The commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 42, verses 32–35:

Verses 32 to 35

The ships that move through the seas like mountains, moving to and fro in the rivers, are further signs among the signs of Allah. This sign too is present and visible. It is a sign that rests upon several of the signs Allah has made, and there is no difference of opinion about it. This sea, apart from Allah, who is it that made it? Humans made it, and the so-called deities made it. Who gave it this depth, this density and this vastness, so that it became capable of bearing great boats and ships? Then, who placed in the material from which ships are made such a property that it floats on the surface of the sea? And then there is the wind which, at that time, drove these ships, and the people of that time, to whom it was addressed, knew it. And in our own age, all the forces which Allah has subjected for humans, and which they employ to run these enormous vessels: who created these forces that drive the modern vessels, which are like mountains upon mountains?

﴿If He wills, He stills the wind, and they remain motionless upon the back of the sea﴾ (42:33). Sometimes these ships would stand still in such a way as though there were no life in them at all.

﴿Indeed, in this there are signs for every person who is greatly patient and grateful﴾ (42:33). That is, there are signs in the sailing of these ships and in their being made to stand still. In the Qur'an, patience and gratitude often come together. Patience is exercised in trial, and gratitude in blessings; joy and sorrow, and patience and gratitude, both move together within human psychology.

﴿Or He destroys them for what they have earned﴾ (42:34). He shatters these boats or drowns them, because people committed sins and disobedience. They opposed faith, although all of Allah's creation is believing, and among humans some deny.

﴿And He pardons much﴾ (42:34). Therefore He does not seize people at every step for every sin, but overlooks and forgives.

﴿And those who dispute concerning Our signs will know that they have no place of escape﴾ (42:35). And if Allah willed, He would place them before His punishment, sink their ships, and they would not be saved... Thus it is made clear to them that the worldly goods and affairs of which they are masters are also within the reach of Allah's destruction. Therefore nothing in this world is lasting or stable, except connection with Allah.

* * *

After this, their attention is drawn to consider how brief is the provision given to them in this world. The true enduring wealth is that which is stored with Allah. And it is for those who believe and place their trust in their Lord. This discourse proceeds further and enumerates the qualities of the believers, which make them a distinct community with its own characteristics, one that is distinguished from all other nations.

﴿If He wills, He stills the wind, and they remain motionless upon the back of the sea﴾ (42:33). Sometimes these ships would stand still in such a way as though there were no life in them at all.

﴿Indeed, in this there are signs for every person who is greatly patient and grateful﴾ (42:33). That is, there are signs in the sailing of these ships and in their being made to stand still. In the Qur'an, patience and gratitude often come together. Patience is exercised in trial, and gratitude in blessings; joy and sorrow, and patience and gratitude, both move together within human psychology.

﴿Or He destroys them for what they have earned﴾ (42:34). He shatters these boats or drowns them, because people committed sins and disobedience. They opposed faith, although all of Allah's creation is believing, and among humans some deny.

﴿And He pardons much﴾ (42:34). Therefore He does not seize people at every step for every sin, but overlooks and forgives.

﴿And those who dispute concerning Our signs will know that they have no place of escape﴾ (42:35). And if Allah willed, He would place them before His punishment, sink their ships, and they would not be saved... Thus it is made clear to them that the worldly goods and affairs of which they are masters are also within the reach of Allah's destruction. Therefore nothing in this world is lasting or stable, except connection with Allah.

* * *

After this, their attention is drawn to consider how brief is the provision given to them in this world. The true enduring wealth is that which is stored with Allah. And it is for those who believe and place their trust in their Lord. This discourse proceeds further and enumerates the qualities of the believers, which make them a distinct community with its own characteristics, one that is distinguished from all other nations.

And if Allah willed, He would place them before His punishment, sink their ships, and they would not be saved... Thus it is made clear to them that the worldly goods and affairs of which they are masters are also within the reach of Allah's destruction. Therefore nothing in this world is lasting or stable, except connection with Allah.

* * *

After this, their attention is drawn to consider how brief is the provision given to them in this world. The true enduring wealth is that which is stored with Allah. And it is for those who believe and place their trust in their Lord. This discourse proceeds further and enumerates the qualities of the believers, which make them a distinct community with its own characteristics, one that is distinguished from all other nations.

The passage opens by recalling that earlier in this surah the Qur'an described how the People of the Book (Ahl al-Kitab) differed among themselves after knowledge had come to them, and that these differences were not born of misunderstanding or ignorance. The clear Book of God had come to them, yet they divided out of envy and enmity. It was also stated that from the time of Noah, Abraham, Moses and Jesus (peace be upon them) God had established for people a heavenly religion (din samawi), a method (minhaj) and a system of life, and had enjoined them to establish it. It was further explained that those who, out of envy and enmity, differed regarding the divine method, and after them the later generations who received a Book, fell into doubt about the Books themselves because of these differences. If this was the condition of the People of the Book and the adherents of heavenly religion, then the condition of the nations that had no Book or religion at all must obviously be worse.

For this reason humanity needed righteous leadership that would bring people out of blind ignorance (jahiliyyah), guide them, and bind them together with a strong rope, directing them towards the path that leads to Allah, the Lord of this existence.

Therefore Allah sent down this final Book in the Arabic language to His last Prophet, Muhammad (ﷺ), so that he might begin the call among the people of Umm al-Qura, Makkah al-Mukarramah, and its surroundings, and establish among them the same religion that had been strictly enjoined upon Noah, Abraham, Moses and Jesus (peace be upon them). The purpose was that the links of all the true religions should join together, so that from the beginning of history until Muhammad (ﷺ) there would be one path, one method, one religion and one law. A community would be established here to safeguard this historic call, to lead it, and to bring this call into being on this earth in accordance with the will of Allah, and to establish this method here in the form that pleases Allah. Accordingly, in the verses under discussion, the features of the community that is to carry out this great obligation are being described.

It should be kept in view that these verses are Makkan and were revealed before the establishment of the Islamic system of government in Madinah. Yet even in Makkah we see one of the distinguishing characteristics of the Islamic movement (Tahrik-i Islami).

"Their affairs are conducted by mutual consultation" (42:38). This shows that the institution of consultation (shura) is an important part of Islamic society and of the life of the Muslims. It is a fundamental characteristic of the Islamic community. The organisation of the community is founded upon consultation, and this system then extends beyond the community to become part of the state. In other words, consultation is the life-blood of the Islamic society, and it spreads throughout it. In this way, the second characteristic of this community is described.

"Those who, when oppression afflicts them, defend themselves" (42:39). Although in Makkah the command had been: be patient, and do not repay evil with evil, and this command was in force until, after the Hijrah, permission for fighting (qital) was granted and it was said:

"Permission is given to those against whom war is being waged, because they have been wronged; and surely Allah is able to give them victory" (22:39).

The mention of this quality in these Makkan verses is therefore because it is the disposition of the Islamic movement to stand firm against oppression. The commands before and after this are for patience and restraint, while this is an exceptional ruling for a specific time. Since in this Makkan surah the fundamental qualities of the Muslim community were being recorded, it was mentioned here that although at present retaliation was prohibited, this quality is nonetheless among the fundamental qualities of the believers.

Nevertheless, to mention within the qualities of the Muslim community matters that were not being practised at that time, when the community did not hold practical leadership of any state and was still enduring hardships in Makkah, was done because this community was to lead all humanity and was established so that it would bring the whole of humanity out of darkness into the light of Islam. Therefore it was necessary that these qualities be developed within the community and that the community be prepared for these purposes. It is necessary to keep these matters in view so that when power comes into its hands it will be fit to wield it. Therefore these qualities require deep reflection: what are they, what is their reality, and what is their importance in human society?

These are the qualities of an Islamic community: faith (iman), reliance upon Allah (tawakkul), avoiding major sins (kaba'ir) and immoralities (fawahish), forgiveness at the time of anger, responding to the call of Allah, establishing prayer (iqamat al-salat), consultation in every matter, spending in the way of Allah (infaq fi sabil Allah), standing against oppression and transgression, pardon, reform, and patience. What are these, what is their reality, and what is their importance? It is appropriate to explain these qualities in the order in which the Qur'an presents them.

The Qur'an places people before the balance (mizan) established by Allah, which is firm and everlasting, so that they may distinguish between permanent and lasting values and temporary, changing circumstances. Their outlook must not be confused, otherwise the true worth of everything will not remain correct in their eyes. Therefore, before describing the qualities of the believers, Allah set out an enduring standard and measure, by which the qualities of a Muslim community are to be judged.

"Whatever you have been given is merely the enjoyment of the life of this world, and what is with Allah is better and more lasting" (42:36). The provisions of this earth are very alluring and dazzling: food and drink, children, desires, pleasures, status, authority and the like. Some blessings are those which Allah has given to His servants on the earth as an act of mercy, and these are pure bounty from Allah. Allah has not made them dependent in this world upon disobedience or obedience. Although a little bounty granted to an obedient person carries blessing, and even if an evildoer holds much, blessing is taken away from it.

But all these matters are not lasting values. They are a provision and the equipment of this life. This equipment is for a limited time. It neither elevates anyone's rank nor lowers it. It is not a proof of nobility and honour before Allah, nor a proof of disapproval and displeasure. It does not show that Allah is pleased with a person, nor does it show that Allah is angry with him. It is simply the provision of this life, this transient life, and in comparison with it:

"And what is with Allah is better and more lasting" (42:36). It is better in its worth, and more lasting because it is everlasting. Therefore the provisions of this transient world, in comparison with the Hereafter, are nothing. They are very limited and of little value, and they last only for a few days. For an individual they are useful only during his own life, and then each person should consider how much of his life he has brought with him and how much remains. And in comparison with the Days of Allah (ayyam Allah), this is very little, indeed like moments, as in the blink of an eye.

After this introductory statement and the explanation of the true criterion of good and evil, Allah now describes the qualities of those believers for whom He has prepared a better and more lasting end with Him.

"And what is with Allah is better and more lasting for those who believe" (42:36). Faith is a reality which, when it settles in the mind, makes it possible for human beings to determine the true "value" of everything in this universe. Only through faith can we grasp the reality of this universe, because the Lord of the worlds has told us about it. Only after grasping this reality can a person deal rightly with this universe. In this way a human being comes to know its reality, is able to understand the laws of nature within it, and can thereby bring his movement into harmony with the movement of this universe. Then a person will not deviate from the universal laws of nature, because such deviation would destroy this harmony, and this harmony is so important that with it a person can live a good life in this world, and together with that great existence can spend his life in obedience and submission to his Creator and Lord. This quality is necessary for every human being, that he be a believer; but the community which is to lead the journey of all humanity, and which is to bring all humanity to the Creator of the universe, must possess this quality to the highest degree.

What are the results of this faith? The believer attains psychological tranquillity and clarity of purpose. Doubt, bewilderment, fear and despair do not come near him, and these qualities are indispensable for ordinary life on this earth. But these qualities are essential for that community which is to guide other human beings along this difficult path.

Among the important values of faith is that the believer is free from base desires, personal aims, individual interests and the pursuit of gain. Only then will he be able to work for a lofty purpose. He will reflect that he has no personal share in this work; it is simply the duty of calling to Allah. He has already received his reward from Allah, and his bargain has been concluded with Allah. This awareness is especially necessary for the one who is the leader of the movement, so that he does not become despondent when a headstrong group separates from him or when he is harmed because of the call, and so that, if the whole public becomes his followers and obeys him, he does not become proud, for he is a labourer who has already taken his wages from Allah.

The truth is that the first group of Muslims, the community of the Companions, developed this kind of faith. Their faith brought about a remarkable revolution in their souls, their morals and their conduct. In their time the very form of faith had become distorted among all humanity. Faith had been suppressed; indeed, faith had no effect at all upon people's morals, conduct and psychology. When Islam came, it gave faith a living, effective and dynamic form, and it produced a group of Companions (may Allah be pleased with them) who took up the banner of the Islamic revolution.

* * *

Sayyid Abul Hasan Ali Nadwi, in his book "The Global Effects of the Decline of the Muslims" (Musalmanon ke Zawal ke Alami Asrat), says:

"This is the faith to which this verse alludes, and in it faith is mentioned as the first quality of the community raised up to lead all humanity, which, through its faith, leads humanity. The demand of this faith is that a believer relies upon Allah alone."

But the Qur'an mentions reliance upon Allah as a separate and independent theme:

"And upon their Lord they rely" (42:36). Here, instead of the ordinary phrase "yatawakkalna 'ala rabbihim", it says "wa 'ala rabbihim yatawakkalun" (42:36). By placing the prepositional phrase ahead of the verb, a sense of restriction (hasr) arises: they rely upon their Lord alone, and upon no one else. This too is the doctrine of Tawhid, and the first requirement of the doctrine of Tawhid is that they rely upon Allah. The believer has faith in the essence and attributes of Allah. He is certain that no person in this universe can do anything by his own will; nothing happens here without the permission of Allah. Therefore the believer relies upon Allah alone. In doing or not doing anything, the believer relies upon Allah alone.

This awareness is indispensable in the practical life of every person, because in this way he walks with his head held high before everyone, and his head does not bow before anyone. He will be very content; he will place no hope in anyone, and will have no fear of anyone. If difficulties come, he will be resolute and steadfast, and if times are good, he will remain sober. Neither prosperity nor adversity will be able to move him from his place. This awareness is very essential for the leader of the Islamic revolution, so that he may remain firm amid the ups and downs of this path, and this quality is also necessary for every member of the community that is bringing about the Islamic revolution.

"And who avoid the major sins and immoralities" (42:37). Purity of heart and a transparent conduct, especially avoidance of major sins and acts of immorality, is a fundamental characteristic of an Islamic society and is among the clear signs of faith. For a true leader, and especially for a community that rises to call to Islam, this is an extremely necessary quality. No heart can remain pure if it commits sins, participates in acts of immorality and does not avoid these things. No individual or community is fit for leadership if its heart is not clean, and if sin and immorality have themselves destroyed its faith and distorted its very form.

In the hearts of the first community of Muslims, faith had risen to such a degree and with such a keen sense of awareness that it is alluded to in the verse mentioned above (22), and in this way faith raised that community to the station of human leadership. They provided a leadership of a kind that is found neither in ancient history nor in modern history. Such leadership is like a sharp arrow that points to a star, in a world where the war of desires rages and there is a state of every man for himself.

Sayyid Qutb's commentary, Fi Zilal al-Quran (Urdu translation), on Surah 42, verses 36–43 (part 2 of 3):

Allah is well aware of the weaknesses of this human creation, so He has also kept the conditions of leadership within a reasonable limit, such that a leadership can act upon them and thereby obtain the reward that is stored with Allah. The standard that Allah has prescribed is that the Islamic community and its leadership should avoid major sins and indecencies. As for minor lapses, Allah will forgive them, because Allah is well aware of the limits and bounds of human obedience. This is the grace, kindness and mercy of Allah that He has shown to this human being. It is appropriate that we feel shame before Allah, because kindness creates feelings of modesty in a person, and forgiveness and pardon create honour and respect.

﴿And when they are angered, they forgive﴾ (42:37). This quality came immediately after a point had already been indicated: that Allah pardons the small sins of His servants and overlooks them. Therefore the servants too should treat one another with kindness and forgiveness. Accordingly, among the qualities of the believers it was included that when they become angry, they forgive one another.

In this matter too, Islam shows immense kindness to the human soul. Islam does not burden a person beyond his capacity. Allah knew that anger is a human reaction that arises from human nature, and that this anger is not purely evil. For the sake of Allah, for the sake of the religion of Allah, for the sake of truth and for the sake of justice, anger is desirable, and there is good in it. Therefore Islam does not declare the mere feeling of anger to be a crime, nor does it call it an error. Rather, Islam accepts anger as part of human temperament and nature. For this reason Islam does not create a separation or division between a person and his nature because of any religious command. Yes, Islam does guide that a person should control his anger. He should, as far as possible, act with pardon and forgiveness, and this will be an exemplary quality among his attributes of faith. In this regard, it is related about the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) that he never became angry over personal matters. His anger was for the sake of Allah, and then no force could withstand his anger. But this is the station and the perfection of the Muhammadan station (ﷺ). Allah commands ordinary Muslims only in accordance with their strength, although He tests them in this too, and He only commands that if anger comes, they should forgive, and if it is possible, they should pardon and control the feelings of vengeance, provided the matter is within personal bounds and is between two individuals.

﴿And those who respond to their Lord﴾ (42:38). They remove the obstacles that stand between them and their Lord, and they erase from the human soul whatever prevents attention toward Allah. These obstacles are the carnal desires, passions and inclinations, and those barriers that are attached to a person's being and self. When a person controls his personal desires and removes personal obstacles, then the path between him and his Lord becomes clear. Then he is ready at all times to carry out every command of his Lord, and no personal desire can become an obstacle before the command of Allah. This is the general quality of acting upon the commands of Allah, but some of the commands of Allah are also specifically mentioned here.

﴿And establish prayer﴾ (42:38). In Islam, prayer holds a very great station and rank. After the affirmation of the Kalimah Tayyibah, the first command that comes is that of prayer. As it were, prayer is the beginning of following the commands of Allah. The connection between the servant and his Lord is called prayer. Furthermore, it is an expression of the fact that in Islam, the high and the low stand in the same rank; no one's head is raised above another's, and no one is ahead of another. This is the aspect of equality, and for this reason, after prayer, zakat is generally mentioned. Here, however, before zakat, ﴿and their affairs are by mutual consultation﴾ (42:38) is mentioned, so that it may be known that everyone's opinion is counted equally.

﴿And their affairs are by mutual consultation﴾ (42:38). The manner of expression is such that all their affairs are the result of consultation; as it were, their entire life is coloured by the hue of consultation. As we have said, this is a Meccan verse, and this command predates even the establishment of an Islamic state. This colour is not, as it were, specific only to governmental affairs; rather, it is the general conduct of an Islamic society, even though the government had not yet been established at that time.

The truth is that the organisation of government in Islam is in fact the organised manifestation of the features of Islamic society, and the Islamic government is also included within the Islamic society. Therefore, the Islamic society runs the Islamic government along the same lines as it runs its general affairs.

For this reason, the process of consultation was ongoing in Islamic society from the very beginning, and the scope of this consultation was far wider than the government and governmental commands. This is in fact a quality of Islamic society, and among the distinguishing qualities of that community which Allah has raised up for the leadership of all humanity, and for leadership it is of very great importance.

As for what the form of shura should be, Islam did not create any iron mould for it. In the circumstances of every time and place, its different form can be prepared, so that this quality, namely the spirit of shura, may be prevalent in Islamic society and also current in Islamic institutions. But it should have no rigid form; rather, the spirit of shura should be present everywhere. That is, this shura is in fact not the name of words and forms, but a quality which, as a result of faith, produces a consultative consciousness and conduct in Islamic society. Some people speak of Islamic institutions in which there is no faith at the core, or in which faith is not deemed necessary; they are doing a futile thing. And this is not a superficial matter, as it will appear at first sight, and especially it will appear to those who have not understood the importance of faith in the Islamic worldview. Because before the Islamic worldview is transferred into institutions and organisations, it contains within it intellectual and psychological realities which affect human thought and the human self. Afterwards these appear in the collective institutions of Islam as principles, taking a followed form, and then the texts come, and they point towards these forms and circumstances. The texts organise these principles; they do not create them, for their creation has already taken place through faith.

Therefore, for the manifestation of any form of the Islamic worldview, the existence of an Islamic society and of Muslims in a country is necessary, and those Muslims' faith must be active and effective. If Muslims do not exist at all, then merely by establishing institutions nothing is achieved. Mere institutions will not fulfil needs, and in that case no system will come into being that could be called Islamic.

When Muslims are truly present and faith comes into being in its reality, then the Islamic system will come into being by itself, and its institutional form will come into being automatically, which will be the need of those Muslims and the need of their society, and only in this way can the true fulfilment of the dream of Islamic principles come into being.

﴿And from what We have provided them, they spend﴾ (42:38). This verse also relates to the period before the command making zakat obligatory. Zakat became obligatory in the second year after the Hijrah, but spending in the way of Allah was a general command for the Islamic community even earlier. Indeed, this command came into existence together with the formation of the Islamic society.

The work of Islamic da'wah requires wealth, and this wealth will be obtained through spending. Through spending, the hearts of people are purified from the bad trait of miserliness, when the human urge for wealth comes under control and one learns to rely upon Allah rather than upon one's possessions. All these matters are necessary for the refinement of the meaning of faith. And it is clear that no collective system can be established without spending, because da'wah is a struggle, and in struggle the maintenance of workers is necessary so that collective needs may be met and results may be produced. At times this mutual support becomes so comprehensive that individuals are not even permitted to keep private wealth. When the Muhajirun left Makkah and, together with the Ansar in Madinah, a system was established, all of this was under this principle. But when conditions returned to normal, then zakat was put into practice and the system of mu'akhah (brotherhood), which was complete mutual support, was abrogated. In any case, spending in the way of Allah is the distinguishing feature of the community chosen for this purpose, or the community established for this purpose, that it should bring about an Islamic revolution in some region.

﴿And those who, when oppression afflicts them, they defend themselves﴾ (42:39). The mention of this quality in the Meccan surahs carries a special meaning within itself, as we said earlier. Through it, the intention is to show that within the Islamic community, the Muslim ummah has this natural quality, that they confront oppression. Confronting evil is an important duty, because if someone lays down his arms before an oppressor, the oppressor becomes more arrogant and bold. Therefore, confronting the oppressor is very necessary. And for a nation that was raised up precisely so that it would guard people's rights, with enjoining good as its mission and forbidding evil as its obligation, confronting evil is extremely important, because the ideal and goal of the Muslim ummah and the Muslim community is to dominate human life and to establish justice and fairness within it in truth.

﴿And honour belongs to Allah, to His Messenger and to the believers﴾. Therefore, the temperament of the Islamic community and the nature of its duties require that it confront oppression and defend itself against the acts of aggression being carried out against it. In Makkah the command was: hold back, restrain your hands and be patient; pray and give zakat. There, these commands were due to the specific circumstances of Makkah, and some training of the early Arab Muslims was also desired, because the Arabs were by temperament vengeful. These were not permanent commands for the Islamic community and Islamic society. In Makkah, for certain special reasons, the command was given that at any cost, peace and security for coexistence should not be allowed to slip away.

1. Because the harshness and oppression against the Muslims did not come from any organised government institution ruling the community of that time, since the political situation of the Arabian Peninsula was of an unorganised tribal nature. There, the persecution of Muslims was carried out, if a Muslim was a member of a tribe, by the tribe, and within the tribe no one but his close relatives would dare to do so. Muslims were not subjected to persecution as a community. Sometimes masters would persecute their Muslim slaves, and Muslims would buy them and set them free. Therefore no one dared to persecute their slaves excessively. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) did not wish that fighting should break out house by house in Makkah, with members of the same household who had become Muslim beginning to fight against non-Muslims. Moreover, in Makkah, gentleness softened the hearts of other people far more than harshness did.

Furthermore, Arab society was a society of self-respect and chivalry. In it, people would rise up in support of the oppressed. When Muslims endured suffering and remained firm upon their belief, the feelings of Arab chivalry would rise on their behalf. During the siege in Shi'b Abi Talib, it was generally that same feeling which helped the Muslims, in which all of Banu Hashim had been besieged. Against this blockade, people's sympathies turned in favour of the Muslims, and people tore to pieces the agreement that was in the document, and thus this unjust pact came to an end.

Moreover, it was the custom among the Arabs to draw the sword at the slightest matter. They were highly emotional and not bound by any discipline or order. The organisation desired in the Islamic community required that this emotionalism be restrained somewhat and be bound to a goal, and that people be made accustomed to nervous self-control and patience, and that a consciousness be created among people that ideology and ultimate aim take precedence over every emotion and every interest. Therefore, in Makkah, the continual exhortation to patience was very necessary for the methodology of Islamic training. In this way, the desired balance came into being in the personality of a Muslim, and they continued to advance with patience and steadfastness towards their goal.... In short, these and other similar reasons are known to Allah and His Messenger. Because of them, in Makkah, the exhortation to patience continued, but the real aim of the Islamic movement was always this.

﴿And those who, when oppression afflicts them, they defend themselves﴾ (42:39).

This principle is practically given effect by another principle of life, namely:

﴿And the recompense for an evil is an evil like it﴾ (42:40). The principle of punishment is that the penalty should be of the same kind as the crime, so that a person does not become rebellious. If a rebellious person has no one to restrain him, then he advances very comfortably in rebellion and oppression.

This is the right to redress of the wronged and the general principle. However, if someone pardons for the sake of reforming his own self, or for the sake of good recompense and reward in the Hereafter, or pardons due to feelings that arise against the Muslim community, then there is an exception to this rule. But forgiveness is considered meaningful only when a person has the power to answer evil with evil. At that time, the pardon carries weight, and the wrongdoer is also reformed, because when the aggressor thinks that the pardon and forgiveness were given purely out of generosity, and that there is no weakness on the part of the one who forgave, then he will feel ashamed, will become remorseful, and will refrain from such conduct in future. And he will think that my opponent has treated me with nobility; he is a high-minded person. And the one who has the ability to take revenge and yet forgives, his heart also becomes pure, because in such circumstances forgiveness and pardon are beneficial for both parties. But if a person is unable to take revenge and forgives, then the situation is: "The beggar's humility is his nature." Therefore, such pardon should not even be called pardon, because there is no pardon there; it is compulsion. And this situation is a mischief-producing situation. As a result, the oppressor becomes more emboldened, and corruption spreads. Consider this verse:

﴿فَمَنْ عَفَا وَأَصْلَحَ فَأَجْرُهُ عَلَى اللَّهِ﴾ (42:40) "So whoever pardons and makes reconciliation, his reward is with Allah."

﴿إِنَّهُ لَا يُحِبُّ الظَّالِمِينَ﴾ (42:40) "Indeed, He does not love wrongdoers."

This is an emphasis on the earlier principle that "the recompense for an evil is an evil like it." The meaning is: either forgive, or if you wish to take retribution, take an equal retribution, and do not exceed the limit.

A second emphasis of the same principle:

﴿وَلَمَنِ انتَصَرَ بَعْدَ ظُلْمِهِ فَأُولَٰئِكَ مَا عَلَيْهِم مِّن سَبِيلٍ﴾ (42:41) ﴿إِنَّمَا السَّبِيلُ عَلَى الَّذِينَ يَظْلِمُونَ النَّاسَ وَيَبْغُونَ فِي الْأَرْضِ بِغَيْرِ الْحَقِّ ۚ أُولَٰئِكَ لَهُمْ عَذَابٌ أَلِيمٌ﴾ (42:42) "And those who take retribution after being wronged, there is no blame upon them. The blame is only upon those who wrong people and transgress upon the earth without right; for them is a painful punishment."

Therefore, whoever defends himself after being wronged and takes an equal retribution for evil, without transgressing, there is no accountability upon him. He is exercising his lawful right. Therefore, no one has any argument against him, nor is it permissible for anyone to obstruct his path. The path should be blocked for those who oppress people and commit injustices on earth without entitlement, because no society can be reformed when an oppressor is oppressing people and there is no one to hold his hand. Where there is a rebel who is inflicting oppression upon people and there is no power to restrain him or to make him submit to retribution, Allah nevertheless threatens such oppressors with a painful punishment. But it is also the duty of the people to hold the oppressor's hand.

Finally, despite individual circumstances and the power of retaliation, attention is again drawn to balance, moderation, self-restraint, patience, and the attitude of goodness. When patience and goodness are truly a form of forgiveness, not humiliation, a genuine kindness, and not something one has been forced into:

﴿وَلَمَن صَبَرَ وَغَفَرَ إِنَّ ذَٰلِكَ لَمِنْ عَزْمِ الْأُمُورِ﴾ (42:43) "But whoever is patient and forgives, indeed that is of the matters requiring determination."

All the guidance and injunctions of this paragraph are based on great moderation and balance. Efforts have been made to protect the human self from grudge and anger on one side, and on the other side, to protect it from weakness, humiliation, and oppression and transgression. And in every condition, the pleasure of Allah is to be kept in view. And it has been explained that patience is, in every case, provision for the journey.

The qualities of the believers mentioned here are the characteristics of that revolutionary community which is to lead all of humanity, and whose aim is the reward of the Hereafter and the pleasure of God, and this is for those who believe and put their trust in their Lord.

After stating that these are the qualities of the believers and that the reward of the Hereafter for them is far better and everlasting, now, by way of contrast, the other side of the picture is presented: the end of some oppressors is also given here, and an announcement of humiliation and loss is made for them.

The passage opens by recalling that earlier in this surah the Qur'an described how the People of the Book (Ahl al-Kitab) differed among themselves after knowledge had come to them, and that these differences were not born of misunderstanding or ignorance. The clear Book of God had come to them, yet they divided out of envy and enmity. It was also stated that from the time of Noah, Abraham, Moses and Jesus (peace be upon them) God had established for people a heavenly religion (din samawi), a method (minhaj) and a system of life, and had enjoined them to establish it. It was further explained that those who, out of envy and enmity, differed regarding the divine method, and after them the later generations who received a Book, fell into doubt about the Books themselves because of these differences. If this was the condition of the People of the Book and the adherents of heavenly religion, then the condition of the nations that had no Book or religion at all must obviously be worse.

For this reason humanity needed righteous leadership that would bring people out of blind ignorance (jahiliyyah), guide them, and bind them together with a strong rope, directing them towards the path that leads to Allah, the Lord of this existence.

Therefore Allah sent down this final Book in the Arabic language to His last Prophet, Muhammad (ﷺ), so that he might begin the call among the people of Umm al-Qura, Makkah al-Mukarramah, and its surroundings, and establish among them the same religion that had been strictly enjoined upon Noah, Abraham, Moses and Jesus (peace be upon them). The purpose was that the links of all the true religions should join together, so that from the beginning of history until Muhammad (ﷺ) there would be one path, one method, one religion and one law. A community would be established here to safeguard this historic call, to lead it, and to bring this call into being on this earth in accordance with the will of Allah, and to establish this method here in the form that pleases Allah. Accordingly, in the verses under discussion, the features of the community that is to carry out this great obligation are being described.

It should be kept in view that these verses are Makkan and were revealed before the establishment of the Islamic system of government in Madinah. Yet even in Makkah we see one of the distinguishing characteristics of the Islamic movement (Tahrik-i Islami).

"Their affairs are conducted by mutual consultation" (42:38). This shows that the institution of consultation (shura) is an important part of Islamic society and of the life of the Muslims. It is a fundamental characteristic of the Islamic community. The organisation of the community is founded upon consultation, and this system then extends beyond the community to become part of the state. In other words, consultation is the life-blood of the Islamic society, and it spreads throughout it. In this way, the second characteristic of this community is described.

"Those who, when oppression afflicts them, defend themselves" (42:39). Although in Makkah the command had been: be patient, and do not repay evil with evil, and this command was in force until, after the Hijrah, permission for fighting (qital) was granted and it was said:

"Permission is given to those against whom war is being waged, because they have been wronged; and surely Allah is able to give them victory" (22:39).

The mention of this quality in these Makkan verses is therefore because it is the disposition of the Islamic movement to stand firm against oppression.
