The commands before and after this are for patience and restraint, while this is an exceptional ruling for a specific time. Since in this Makkan surah the fundamental qualities of the Muslim community were being recorded, it was mentioned here that although at present retaliation was prohibited, this quality is nonetheless among the fundamental qualities of the believers.

Nevertheless, to mention within the qualities of the Muslim community matters that were not being practised at that time, when the community did not hold practical leadership of any state and was still enduring hardships in Makkah, was done because this community was to lead all humanity and was established so that it would bring the whole of humanity out of darkness into the light of Islam. Therefore it was necessary that these qualities be developed within the community and that the community be prepared for these purposes. It is necessary to keep these matters in view so that when power comes into its hands it will be fit to wield it. Therefore these qualities require deep reflection: what are they, what is their reality, and what is their importance in human society?

These are the qualities of an Islamic community: faith (iman), reliance upon Allah (tawakkul), avoiding major sins (kaba'ir) and immoralities (fawahish), forgiveness at the time of anger, responding to the call of Allah, establishing prayer (iqamat al-salat), consultation in every matter, spending in the way of Allah (infaq fi sabil Allah), standing against oppression and transgression, pardon, reform, and patience. What are these, what is their reality, and what is their importance? It is appropriate to explain these qualities in the order in which the Qur'an presents them.

The Qur'an places people before the balance (mizan) established by Allah, which is firm and everlasting, so that they may distinguish between permanent and lasting values and temporary, changing circumstances. Their outlook must not be confused, otherwise the true worth of everything will not remain correct in their eyes. Therefore, before describing the qualities of the believers, Allah set out an enduring standard and measure, by which the qualities of a Muslim community are to be judged.

"Whatever you have been given is merely the enjoyment of the life of this world, and what is with Allah is better and more lasting" (42:36). The provisions of this earth are very alluring and dazzling: food and drink, children, desires, pleasures, status, authority and the like. Some blessings are those which Allah has given to His servants on the earth as an act of mercy, and these are pure bounty from Allah. Allah has not made them dependent in this world upon disobedience or obedience. Although a little bounty granted to an obedient person carries blessing, and even if an evildoer holds much, blessing is taken away from it.

But all these matters are not lasting values. They are a provision and the equipment of this life. This equipment is for a limited time. It neither elevates anyone's rank nor lowers it. It is not a proof of nobility and honour before Allah, nor a proof of disapproval and displeasure. It does not show that Allah is pleased with a person, nor does it show that Allah is angry with him. It is simply the provision of this life, this transient life, and in comparison with it:

"And what is with Allah is better and more lasting" (42:36). It is better in its worth, and more lasting because it is everlasting. Therefore the provisions of this transient world, in comparison with the Hereafter, are nothing. They are very limited and of little value, and they last only for a few days. For an individual they are useful only during his own life, and then each person should consider how much of his life he has brought with him and how much remains. And in comparison with the Days of Allah (ayyam Allah), this is very little, indeed like moments, as in the blink of an eye.

After this introductory statement and the explanation of the true criterion of good and evil, Allah now describes the qualities of those believers for whom He has prepared a better and more lasting end with Him.

"And what is with Allah is better and more lasting for those who believe" (42:36). Faith is a reality which, when it settles in the mind, makes it possible for human beings to determine the true "value" of everything in this universe. Only through faith can we grasp the reality of this universe, because the Lord of the worlds has told us about it. Only after grasping this reality can a person deal rightly with this universe. In this way a human being comes to know its reality, is able to understand the laws of nature within it, and can thereby bring his movement into harmony with the movement of this universe. Then a person will not deviate from the universal laws of nature, because such deviation would destroy this harmony, and this harmony is so important that with it a person can live a good life in this world, and together with that great existence can spend his life in obedience and submission to his Creator and Lord. This quality is necessary for every human being, that he be a believer; but the community which is to lead the journey of all humanity, and which is to bring all humanity to the Creator of the universe, must possess this quality to the highest degree.

What are the results of this faith? The believer attains psychological tranquillity and clarity of purpose. Doubt, bewilderment, fear and despair do not come near him, and these qualities are indispensable for ordinary life on this earth. But these qualities are essential for that community which is to guide other human beings along this difficult path.

Among the important values of faith is that the believer is free from base desires, personal aims, individual interests and the pursuit of gain. Only then will he be able to work for a lofty purpose. He will reflect that he has no personal share in this work; it is simply the duty of calling to Allah. He has already received his reward from Allah, and his bargain has been concluded with Allah. This awareness is especially necessary for the one who is the leader of the movement, so that he does not become despondent when a headstrong group separates from him or when he is harmed because of the call, and so that, if the whole public becomes his followers and obeys him, he does not become proud, for he is a labourer who has already taken his wages from Allah.

The truth is that the first group of Muslims, the community of the Companions, developed this kind of faith. Their faith brought about a remarkable revolution in their souls, their morals and their conduct. In their time the very form of faith had become distorted among all humanity. Faith had been suppressed; indeed, faith had no effect at all upon people's morals, conduct and psychology. When Islam came, it gave faith a living, effective and dynamic form, and it produced a group of Companions (may Allah be pleased with them) who took up the banner of the Islamic revolution.

* * *

Sayyid Abul Hasan Ali Nadwi, in his book "The Global Effects of the Decline of the Muslims" (Musalmanon ke Zawal ke Alami Asrat), says:

"This is the faith to which this verse alludes, and in it faith is mentioned as the first quality of the community raised up to lead all humanity, which, through its faith, leads humanity. The demand of this faith is that a believer relies upon Allah alone."

But the Qur'an mentions reliance upon Allah as a separate and independent theme:

"And upon their Lord they rely" (42:36). Here, instead of the ordinary phrase "yatawakkalna 'ala rabbihim", it says "wa 'ala rabbihim yatawakkalun" (42:36). By placing the prepositional phrase ahead of the verb, a sense of restriction (hasr) arises: they rely upon their Lord alone, and upon no one else. This too is the doctrine of Tawhid, and the first requirement of the doctrine of Tawhid is that they rely upon Allah. The believer has faith in the essence and attributes of Allah. He is certain that no person in this universe can do anything by his own will; nothing happens here without the permission of Allah. Therefore the believer relies upon Allah alone. In doing or not doing anything, the believer relies upon Allah alone.

This awareness is indispensable in the practical life of every person, because in this way he walks with his head held high before everyone, and his head does not bow before anyone. He will be very content; he will place no hope in anyone, and will have no fear of anyone. If difficulties come, he will be resolute and steadfast, and if times are good, he will remain sober. Neither prosperity nor adversity will be able to move him from his place. This awareness is very essential for the leader of the Islamic revolution, so that he may remain firm amid the ups and downs of this path, and this quality is also necessary for every member of the community that is bringing about the Islamic revolution.

"And who avoid the major sins and immoralities" (42:37). Purity of heart and a transparent conduct, especially avoidance of major sins and acts of immorality, is a fundamental characteristic of an Islamic society and is among the clear signs of faith. For a true leader, and especially for a community that rises to call to Islam, this is an extremely necessary quality. No heart can remain pure if it commits sins, participates in acts of immorality and does not avoid these things. No individual or community is fit for leadership if its heart is not clean, and if sin and immorality have themselves destroyed its faith and distorted its very form.

In the hearts of the first community of Muslims, faith had risen to such a degree and with such a keen sense of awareness that it is alluded to in the verse mentioned above (22), and in this way faith raised that community to the station of human leadership. They provided a leadership of a kind that is found neither in ancient history nor in modern history. Such leadership is like a sharp arrow that points to a star, in a world where the war of desires rages and there is a state of every man for himself.

Sayyid Qutb's commentary, Fi Zilal al-Quran (Urdu translation), on Surah 42, verses 36–43 (part 2 of 3):

Allah is well aware of the weaknesses of this human creation, so He has also kept the conditions of leadership within a reasonable limit, such that a leadership can act upon them and thereby obtain the reward that is stored with Allah. The standard that Allah has prescribed is that the Islamic community and its leadership should avoid major sins and indecencies. As for minor lapses, Allah will forgive them, because Allah is well aware of the limits and bounds of human obedience. This is the grace, kindness and mercy of Allah that He has shown to this human being. It is appropriate that we feel shame before Allah, because kindness creates feelings of modesty in a person, and forgiveness and pardon create honour and respect.

﴿And when they are angered, they forgive﴾ (42:37). This quality came immediately after a point had already been indicated: that Allah pardons the small sins of His servants and overlooks them. Therefore the servants too should treat one another with kindness and forgiveness. Accordingly, among the qualities of the believers it was included that when they become angry, they forgive one another.

In this matter too, Islam shows immense kindness to the human soul. Islam does not burden a person beyond his capacity. Allah knew that anger is a human reaction that arises from human nature, and that this anger is not purely evil. For the sake of Allah, for the sake of the religion of Allah, for the sake of truth and for the sake of justice, anger is desirable, and there is good in it. Therefore Islam does not declare the mere feeling of anger to be a crime, nor does it call it an error. Rather, Islam accepts anger as part of human temperament and nature. For this reason Islam does not create a separation or division between a person and his nature because of any religious command. Yes, Islam does guide that a person should control his anger. He should, as far as possible, act with pardon and forgiveness, and this will be an exemplary quality among his attributes of faith. In this regard, it is related about the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) that he never became angry over personal matters. His anger was for the sake of Allah, and then no force could withstand his anger. But this is the station and the perfection of the Muhammadan station (ﷺ). Allah commands ordinary Muslims only in accordance with their strength, although He tests them in this too, and He only commands that if anger comes, they should forgive, and if it is possible, they should pardon and control the feelings of vengeance, provided the matter is within personal bounds and is between two individuals.

﴿And those who respond to their Lord﴾ (42:38). They remove the obstacles that stand between them and their Lord, and they erase from the human soul whatever prevents attention toward Allah. These obstacles are the carnal desires, passions and inclinations, and those barriers that are attached to a person's being and self. When a person controls his personal desires and removes personal obstacles, then the path between him and his Lord becomes clear. Then he is ready at all times to carry out every command of his Lord, and no personal desire can become an obstacle before the command of Allah. This is the general quality of acting upon the commands of Allah, but some of the commands of Allah are also specifically mentioned here.

﴿And establish prayer﴾ (42:38). In Islam, prayer holds a very great station and rank. After the affirmation of the Kalimah Tayyibah, the first command that comes is that of prayer. As it were, prayer is the beginning of following the commands of Allah. The connection between the servant and his Lord is called prayer. Furthermore, it is an expression of the fact that in Islam, the high and the low stand in the same rank; no one's head is raised above another's, and no one is ahead of another. This is the aspect of equality, and for this reason, after prayer, zakat is generally mentioned. Here, however, before zakat, ﴿and their affairs are by mutual consultation﴾ (42:38) is mentioned, so that it may be known that everyone's opinion is counted equally.

﴿And their affairs are by mutual consultation﴾ (42:38). The manner of expression is such that all their affairs are the result of consultation; as it were, their entire life is coloured by the hue of consultation. As we have said, this is a Meccan verse, and this command predates even the establishment of an Islamic state. This colour is not, as it were, specific only to governmental affairs; rather, it is the general conduct of an Islamic society, even though the government had not yet been established at that time.

The truth is that the organisation of government in Islam is in fact the organised manifestation of the features of Islamic society, and the Islamic government is also included within the Islamic society. Therefore, the Islamic society runs the Islamic government along the same lines as it runs its general affairs.

For this reason, the process of consultation was ongoing in Islamic society from the very beginning, and the scope of this consultation was far wider than the government and governmental commands. This is in fact a quality of Islamic society, and among the distinguishing qualities of that community which Allah has raised up for the leadership of all humanity, and for leadership it is of very great importance.

As for what the form of shura should be, Islam did not create any iron mould for it. In the circumstances of every time and place, its different form can be prepared, so that this quality, namely the spirit of shura, may be prevalent in Islamic society and also current in Islamic institutions. But it should have no rigid form; rather, the spirit of shura should be present everywhere. That is, this shura is in fact not the name of words and forms, but a quality which, as a result of faith, produces a consultative consciousness and conduct in Islamic society. Some people speak of Islamic institutions in which there is no faith at the core, or in which faith is not deemed necessary; they are doing a futile thing. And this is not a superficial matter, as it will appear at first sight, and especially it will appear to those who have not understood the importance of faith in the Islamic worldview. Because before the Islamic worldview is transferred into institutions and organisations, it contains within it intellectual and psychological realities which affect human thought and the human self. Afterwards these appear in the collective institutions of Islam as principles, taking a followed form, and then the texts come, and they point towards these forms and circumstances. The texts organise these principles; they do not create them, for their creation has already taken place through faith.

Therefore, for the manifestation of any form of the Islamic worldview, the existence of an Islamic society and of Muslims in a country is necessary, and those Muslims' faith must be active and effective. If Muslims do not exist at all, then merely by establishing institutions nothing is achieved. Mere institutions will not fulfil needs, and in that case no system will come into being that could be called Islamic.

When Muslims are truly present and faith comes into being in its reality, then the Islamic system will come into being by itself, and its institutional form will come into being automatically, which will be the need of those Muslims and the need of their society, and only in this way can the true fulfilment of the dream of Islamic principles come into being.

﴿And from what We have provided them, they spend﴾ (42:38). This verse also relates to the period before the command making zakat obligatory. Zakat became obligatory in the second year after the Hijrah, but spending in the way of Allah was a general command for the Islamic community even earlier. Indeed, this command came into existence together with the formation of the Islamic society.

The work of Islamic da'wah requires wealth, and this wealth will be obtained through spending. Through spending, the hearts of people are purified from the bad trait of miserliness, when the human urge for wealth comes under control and one learns to rely upon Allah rather than upon one's possessions. All these matters are necessary for the refinement of the meaning of faith. And it is clear that no collective system can be established without spending, because da'wah is a struggle, and in struggle the maintenance of workers is necessary so that collective needs may be met and results may be produced. At times this mutual support becomes so comprehensive that individuals are not even permitted to keep private wealth. When the Muhajirun left Makkah and, together with the Ansar in Madinah, a system was established, all of this was under this principle. But when conditions returned to normal, then zakat was put into practice and the system of mu'akhah (brotherhood), which was complete mutual support, was abrogated. In any case, spending in the way of Allah is the distinguishing feature of the community chosen for this purpose, or the community established for this purpose, that it should bring about an Islamic revolution in some region.

﴿And those who, when oppression afflicts them, they defend themselves﴾ (42:39). The mention of this quality in the Meccan surahs carries a special meaning within itself, as we said earlier. Through it, the intention is to show that within the Islamic community, the Muslim ummah has this natural quality, that they confront oppression. Confronting evil is an important duty, because if someone lays down his arms before an oppressor, the oppressor becomes more arrogant and bold. Therefore, confronting the oppressor is very necessary. And for a nation that was raised up precisely so that it would guard people's rights, with enjoining good as its mission and forbidding evil as its obligation, confronting evil is extremely important, because the ideal and goal of the Muslim ummah and the Muslim community is to dominate human life and to establish justice and fairness within it in truth.

﴿And honour belongs to Allah, to His Messenger and to the believers﴾. Therefore, the temperament of the Islamic community and the nature of its duties require that it confront oppression and defend itself against the acts of aggression being carried out against it. In Makkah the command was: hold back, restrain your hands and be patient; pray and give zakat. There, these commands were due to the specific circumstances of Makkah, and some training of the early Arab Muslims was also desired, because the Arabs were by temperament vengeful. These were not permanent commands for the Islamic community and Islamic society. In Makkah, for certain special reasons, the command was given that at any cost, peace and security for coexistence should not be allowed to slip away.

1. Because the harshness and oppression against the Muslims did not come from any organised government institution ruling the community of that time, since the political situation of the Arabian Peninsula was of an unorganised tribal nature. There, the persecution of Muslims was carried out, if a Muslim was a member of a tribe, by the tribe, and within the tribe no one but his close relatives would dare to do so. Muslims were not subjected to persecution as a community. Sometimes masters would persecute their Muslim slaves, and Muslims would buy them and set them free. Therefore no one dared to persecute their slaves excessively. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) did not wish that fighting should break out house by house in Makkah, with members of the same household who had become Muslim beginning to fight against non-Muslims. Moreover, in Makkah, gentleness softened the hearts of other people far more than harshness did.

Furthermore, Arab society was a society of self-respect and chivalry. In it, people would rise up in support of the oppressed. When Muslims endured suffering and remained firm upon their belief, the feelings of Arab chivalry would rise on their behalf. During the siege in Shi'b Abi Talib, it was generally that same feeling which helped the Muslims, in which all of Banu Hashim had been besieged. Against this blockade, people's sympathies turned in favour of the Muslims, and people tore to pieces the agreement that was in the document, and thus this unjust pact came to an end.

Moreover, it was the custom among the Arabs to draw the sword at the slightest matter. They were highly emotional and not bound by any discipline or order. The organisation desired in the Islamic community required that this emotionalism be restrained somewhat and be bound to a goal, and that people be made accustomed to nervous self-control and patience, and that a consciousness be created among people that ideology and ultimate aim take precedence over every emotion and every interest. Therefore, in Makkah, the continual exhortation to patience was very necessary for the methodology of Islamic training. In this way, the desired balance came into being in the personality of a Muslim, and they continued to advance with patience and steadfastness towards their goal.... In short, these and other similar reasons are known to Allah and His Messenger. Because of them, in Makkah, the exhortation to patience continued, but the real aim of the Islamic movement was always this.

﴿And those who, when oppression afflicts them, they defend themselves﴾ (42:39).

This principle is practically given effect by another principle of life, namely:

﴿And the recompense for an evil is an evil like it﴾ (42:40). The principle of punishment is that the penalty should be of the same kind as the crime, so that a person does not become rebellious. If a rebellious person has no one to restrain him, then he advances very comfortably in rebellion and oppression.

This is the right to redress of the wronged and the general principle. However, if someone pardons for the sake of reforming his own self, or for the sake of good recompense and reward in the Hereafter, or pardons due to feelings that arise against the Muslim community, then there is an exception to this rule. But forgiveness is considered meaningful only when a person has the power to answer evil with evil. At that time, the pardon carries weight, and the wrongdoer is also reformed, because when the aggressor thinks that the pardon and forgiveness were given purely out of generosity, and that there is no weakness on the part of the one who forgave, then he will feel ashamed, will become remorseful, and will refrain from such conduct in future. And he will think that my opponent has treated me with nobility; he is a high-minded person. And the one who has the ability to take revenge and yet forgives, his heart also becomes pure, because in such circumstances forgiveness and pardon are beneficial for both parties. But if a person is unable to take revenge and forgives, then the situation is: "The beggar's humility is his nature." Therefore, such pardon should not even be called pardon, because there is no pardon there; it is compulsion. And this situation is a mischief-producing situation. As a result, the oppressor becomes more emboldened, and corruption spreads. Consider this verse:

﴿فَمَنْ عَفَا وَأَصْلَحَ فَأَجْرُهُ عَلَى اللَّهِ﴾ (42:40) "So whoever pardons and makes reconciliation, his reward is with Allah."

﴿إِنَّهُ لَا يُحِبُّ الظَّالِمِينَ﴾ (42:40) "Indeed, He does not love wrongdoers."

This is an emphasis on the earlier principle that "the recompense for an evil is an evil like it." The meaning is: either forgive, or if you wish to take retribution, take an equal retribution, and do not exceed the limit.

A second emphasis of the same principle:

﴿وَلَمَنِ انتَصَرَ بَعْدَ ظُلْمِهِ فَأُولَٰئِكَ مَا عَلَيْهِم مِّن سَبِيلٍ﴾ (42:41) ﴿إِنَّمَا السَّبِيلُ عَلَى الَّذِينَ يَظْلِمُونَ النَّاسَ وَيَبْغُونَ فِي الْأَرْضِ بِغَيْرِ الْحَقِّ ۚ أُولَٰئِكَ لَهُمْ عَذَابٌ أَلِيمٌ﴾ (42:42) "And those who take retribution after being wronged, there is no blame upon them. The blame is only upon those who wrong people and transgress upon the earth without right; for them is a painful punishment."

Therefore, whoever defends himself after being wronged and takes an equal retribution for evil, without transgressing, there is no accountability upon him. He is exercising his lawful right. Therefore, no one has any argument against him, nor is it permissible for anyone to obstruct his path. The path should be blocked for those who oppress people and commit injustices on earth without entitlement, because no society can be reformed when an oppressor is oppressing people and there is no one to hold his hand. Where there is a rebel who is inflicting oppression upon people and there is no power to restrain him or to make him submit to retribution, Allah nevertheless threatens such oppressors with a painful punishment. But it is also the duty of the people to hold the oppressor's hand.

Finally, despite individual circumstances and the power of retaliation, attention is again drawn to balance, moderation, self-restraint, patience, and the attitude of goodness. When patience and goodness are truly a form of forgiveness, not humiliation, a genuine kindness, and not something one has been forced into:

﴿وَلَمَن صَبَرَ وَغَفَرَ إِنَّ ذَٰلِكَ لَمِنْ عَزْمِ الْأُمُورِ﴾ (42:43) "But whoever is patient and forgives, indeed that is of the matters requiring determination."

All the guidance and injunctions of this paragraph are based on great moderation and balance. Efforts have been made to protect the human self from grudge and anger on one side, and on the other side, to protect it from weakness, humiliation, and oppression and transgression. And in every condition, the pleasure of Allah is to be kept in view. And it has been explained that patience is, in every case, provision for the journey.

The qualities of the believers mentioned here are the characteristics of that revolutionary community which is to lead all of humanity, and whose aim is the reward of the Hereafter and the pleasure of God, and this is for those who believe and put their trust in their Lord.

After stating that these are the qualities of the believers and that the reward of the Hereafter for them is far better and everlasting, now, by way of contrast, the other side of the picture is presented: the end of some oppressors is also given here, and an announcement of humiliation and loss is made for them.

The passage opens by recalling that earlier in this surah the Qur'an described how the People of the Book (Ahl al-Kitab) differed among themselves after knowledge had come to them, and that these differences were not born of misunderstanding or ignorance. The clear Book of God had come to them, yet they divided out of envy and enmity. It was also stated that from the time of Noah, Abraham, Moses and Jesus (peace be upon them) God had established for people a heavenly religion (din samawi), a method (minhaj) and a system of life, and had enjoined them to establish it. It was further explained that those who, out of envy and enmity, differed regarding the divine method, and after them the later generations who received a Book, fell into doubt about the Books themselves because of these differences. If this was the condition of the People of the Book and the adherents of heavenly religion, then the condition of the nations that had no Book or religion at all must obviously be worse.

For this reason humanity needed righteous leadership that would bring people out of blind ignorance (jahiliyyah), guide them, and bind them together with a strong rope, directing them towards the path that leads to Allah, the Lord of this existence.

Therefore Allah sent down this final Book in the Arabic language to His last Prophet, Muhammad (ﷺ), so that he might begin the call among the people of Umm al-Qura, Makkah al-Mukarramah, and its surroundings, and establish among them the same religion that had been strictly enjoined upon Noah, Abraham, Moses and Jesus (peace be upon them). The purpose was that the links of all the true religions should join together, so that from the beginning of history until Muhammad (ﷺ) there would be one path, one method, one religion and one law. A community would be established here to safeguard this historic call, to lead it, and to bring this call into being on this earth in accordance with the will of Allah, and to establish this method here in the form that pleases Allah. Accordingly, in the verses under discussion, the features of the community that is to carry out this great obligation are being described.

It should be kept in view that these verses are Makkan and were revealed before the establishment of the Islamic system of government in Madinah. Yet even in Makkah we see one of the distinguishing characteristics of the Islamic movement (Tahrik-i Islami).

"Their affairs are conducted by mutual consultation" (42:38). This shows that the institution of consultation (shura) is an important part of Islamic society and of the life of the Muslims. It is a fundamental characteristic of the Islamic community. The organisation of the community is founded upon consultation, and this system then extends beyond the community to become part of the state. In other words, consultation is the life-blood of the Islamic society, and it spreads throughout it. In this way, the second characteristic of this community is described.

"Those who, when oppression afflicts them, defend themselves" (42:39). Although in Makkah the command had been: be patient, and do not repay evil with evil, and this command was in force until, after the Hijrah, permission for fighting (qital) was granted and it was said:

"Permission is given to those against whom war is being waged, because they have been wronged; and surely Allah is able to give them victory" (22:39).

The mention of this quality in these Makkan verses is therefore because it is the disposition of the Islamic movement to stand firm against oppression. The commands before and after this are for patience and restraint, while this is an exceptional ruling for a specific time. Since in this Makkan surah the fundamental qualities of the Muslim community were being recorded, it was mentioned here that although at present retaliation was prohibited, this quality is nonetheless among the fundamental qualities of the believers.

Nevertheless, to mention within the qualities of the Muslim community matters that were not being practised at that time, when the community did not hold practical leadership of any state and was still enduring hardships in Makkah, was done because this community was to lead all humanity and was established so that it would bring the whole of humanity out of darkness into the light of Islam. Therefore it was necessary that these qualities be developed within the community and that the community be prepared for these purposes. It is necessary to keep these matters in view so that when power comes into its hands it will be fit to wield it. Therefore these qualities require deep reflection: what are they, what is their reality, and what is their importance in human society?

These are the qualities of an Islamic community: faith (iman), reliance upon Allah (tawakkul), avoiding major sins (kaba'ir) and immoralities (fawahish), forgiveness at the time of anger, responding to the call of Allah, establishing prayer (iqamat al-salat), consultation in every matter, spending in the way of Allah (infaq fi sabil Allah), standing against oppression and transgression, pardon, reform, and patience. What are these, what is their reality, and what is their importance? It is appropriate to explain these qualities in the order in which the Qur'an presents them.

The Qur'an places people before the balance (mizan) established by Allah, which is firm and everlasting, so that they may distinguish between permanent and lasting values and temporary, changing circumstances. Their outlook must not be confused, otherwise the true worth of everything will not remain correct in their eyes. Therefore, before describing the qualities of the believers, Allah set out an enduring standard and measure, by which the qualities of a Muslim community are to be judged.

"Whatever you have been given is merely the enjoyment of the life of this world, and what is with Allah is better and more lasting" (42:36). The provisions of this earth are very alluring and dazzling: food and drink, children, desires, pleasures, status, authority and the like. Some blessings are those which Allah has given to His servants on the earth as an act of mercy, and these are pure bounty from Allah. Allah has not made them dependent in this world upon disobedience or obedience. Although a little bounty granted to an obedient person carries blessing, and even if an evildoer holds much, blessing is taken away from it.

But all these matters are not lasting values. They are a provision and the equipment of this life. This equipment is for a limited time. It neither elevates anyone's rank nor lowers it. It is not a proof of nobility and honour before Allah, nor a proof of disapproval and displeasure. It does not show that Allah is pleased with a person, nor does it show that Allah is angry with him. It is simply the provision of this life, this transient life, and in comparison with it:

"And what is with Allah is better and more lasting" (42:36). It is better in its worth, and more lasting because it is everlasting. Therefore the provisions of this transient world, in comparison with the Hereafter, are nothing. They are very limited and of little value, and they last only for a few days. For an individual they are useful only during his own life, and then each person should consider how much of his life he has brought with him and how much remains. And in comparison with the Days of Allah (ayyam Allah), this is very little, indeed like moments, as in the blink of an eye.

After this introductory statement and the explanation of the true criterion of good and evil, Allah now describes the qualities of those believers for whom He has prepared a better and more lasting end with Him.

"And what is with Allah is better and more lasting for those who believe" (42:36). Faith is a reality which, when it settles in the mind, makes it possible for human beings to determine the true "value" of everything in this universe. Only through faith can we grasp the reality of this universe, because the Lord of the worlds has told us about it. Only after grasping this reality can a person deal rightly with this universe. In this way a human being comes to know its reality, is able to understand the laws of nature within it, and can thereby bring his movement into harmony with the movement of this universe. Then a person will not deviate from the universal laws of nature, because such deviation would destroy this harmony, and this harmony is so important that with it a person can live a good life in this world, and together with that great existence can spend his life in obedience and submission to his Creator and Lord. This quality is necessary for every human being, that he be a believer; but the community which is to lead the journey of all humanity, and which is to bring all humanity to the Creator of the universe, must possess this quality to the highest degree.

What are the results of this faith? The believer attains psychological tranquillity and clarity of purpose. Doubt, bewilderment, fear and despair do not come near him, and these qualities are indispensable for ordinary life on this earth. But these qualities are essential for that community which is to guide other human beings along this difficult path.

Among the important values of faith is that the believer is free from base desires, personal aims, individual interests and the pursuit of gain. Only then will he be able to work for a lofty purpose. He will reflect that he has no personal share in this work; it is simply the duty of calling to Allah. He has already received his reward from Allah, and his bargain has been concluded with Allah. This awareness is especially necessary for the one who is the leader of the movement, so that he does not become despondent when a headstrong group separates from him or when he is harmed because of the call, and so that, if the whole public becomes his followers and obeys him, he does not become proud, for he is a labourer who has already taken his wages from Allah.

The truth is that the first group of Muslims, the community of the Companions, developed this kind of faith. Their faith brought about a remarkable revolution in their souls, their morals and their conduct. In their time the very form of faith had become distorted among all humanity. Faith had been suppressed; indeed, faith had no effect at all upon people's morals, conduct and psychology. When Islam came, it gave faith a living, effective and dynamic form, and it produced a group of Companions (may Allah be pleased with them) who took up the banner of the Islamic revolution.

* * *

Sayyid Abul Hasan Ali Nadwi, in his book "The Global Effects of the Decline of the Muslims" (Musalmanon ke Zawal ke Alami Asrat), says:

"This is the faith to which this verse alludes, and in it faith is mentioned as the first quality of the community raised up to lead all humanity, which, through its faith, leads humanity. The demand of this faith is that a believer relies upon Allah alone."

But the Qur'an mentions reliance upon Allah as a separate and independent theme:

"And upon their Lord they rely" (42:36). Here, instead of the ordinary phrase "yatawakkalna 'ala rabbihim", it says "wa 'ala rabbihim yatawakkalun" (42:36). By placing the prepositional phrase ahead of the verb, a sense of restriction (hasr) arises: they rely upon their Lord alone, and upon no one else. This too is the doctrine of Tawhid, and the first requirement of the doctrine of Tawhid is that they rely upon Allah. The believer has faith in the essence and attributes of Allah. He is certain that no person in this universe can do anything by his own will; nothing happens here without the permission of Allah. Therefore the believer relies upon Allah alone. In doing or not doing anything, the believer relies upon Allah alone.

This awareness is indispensable in the practical life of every person, because in this way he walks with his head held high before everyone, and his head does not bow before anyone. He will be very content; he will place no hope in anyone, and will have no fear of anyone. If difficulties come, he will be resolute and steadfast, and if times are good, he will remain sober. Neither prosperity nor adversity will be able to move him from his place. This awareness is very essential for the leader of the Islamic revolution, so that he may remain firm amid the ups and downs of this path, and this quality is also necessary for every member of the community that is bringing about the Islamic revolution.

"And who avoid the major sins and immoralities" (42:37). Purity of heart and a transparent conduct, especially avoidance of major sins and acts of immorality, is a fundamental characteristic of an Islamic society and is among the clear signs of faith. For a true leader, and especially for a community that rises to call to Islam, this is an extremely necessary quality. No heart can remain pure if it commits sins, participates in acts of immorality and does not avoid these things. No individual or community is fit for leadership if its heart is not clean, and if sin and immorality have themselves destroyed its faith and distorted its very form.

In the hearts of the first community of Muslims, faith had risen to such a degree and with such a keen sense of awareness that it is alluded to in the verse mentioned above (22), and in this way faith raised that community to the station of human leadership. They provided a leadership of a kind that is found neither in ancient history nor in modern history. Such leadership is like a sharp arrow that points to a star, in a world where the war of desires rages and there is a state of every man for himself.

Sayyid Qutb's commentary, Fi Zilal al-Quran (Urdu translation), on Surah 42, verses 36–43 (part 2 of 3):

Allah is well aware of the weaknesses of this human creation, so He has also kept the conditions of leadership within a reasonable limit, such that a leadership can act upon them and thereby obtain the reward that is stored with Allah. The standard that Allah has prescribed is that the Islamic community and its leadership should avoid major sins and indecencies. As for minor lapses, Allah will forgive them, because Allah is well aware of the limits and bounds of human obedience. This is the grace, kindness and mercy of Allah that He has shown to this human being. It is appropriate that we feel shame before Allah, because kindness creates feelings of modesty in a person, and forgiveness and pardon create honour and respect.

﴿And when they are angered, they forgive﴾ (42:37). This quality came immediately after a point had already been indicated: that Allah pardons the small sins of His servants and overlooks them. Therefore the servants too should treat one another with kindness and forgiveness. Accordingly, among the qualities of the believers it was included that when they become angry, they forgive one another.

In this matter too, Islam shows immense kindness to the human soul. Islam does not burden a person beyond his capacity. Allah knew that anger is a human reaction that arises from human nature, and that this anger is not purely evil. For the sake of Allah, for the sake of the religion of Allah, for the sake of truth and for the sake of justice, anger is desirable, and there is good in it. Therefore Islam does not declare the mere feeling of anger to be a crime, nor does it call it an error. Rather, Islam accepts anger as part of human temperament and nature. For this reason Islam does not create a separation or division between a person and his nature because of any religious command. Yes, Islam does guide that a person should control his anger. He should, as far as possible, act with pardon and forgiveness, and this will be an exemplary quality among his attributes of faith. In this regard, it is related about the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) that he never became angry over personal matters. His anger was for the sake of Allah, and then no force could withstand his anger. But this is the station and the perfection of the Muhammadan station (ﷺ). Allah commands ordinary Muslims only in accordance with their strength, although He tests them in this too, and He only commands that if anger comes, they should forgive, and if it is possible, they should pardon and control the feelings of vengeance, provided the matter is within personal bounds and is between two individuals.

﴿And those who respond to their Lord﴾ (42:38). They remove the obstacles that stand between them and their Lord, and they erase from the human soul whatever prevents attention toward Allah. These obstacles are the carnal desires, passions and inclinations, and those barriers that are attached to a person's being and self. When a person controls his personal desires and removes personal obstacles, then the path between him and his Lord becomes clear. Then he is ready at all times to carry out every command of his Lord, and no personal desire can become an obstacle before the command of Allah. This is the general quality of acting upon the commands of Allah, but some of the commands of Allah are also specifically mentioned here.

﴿And establish prayer﴾ (42:38). In Islam, prayer holds a very great station and rank. After the affirmation of the Kalimah Tayyibah, the first command that comes is that of prayer. As it were, prayer is the beginning of following the commands of Allah. The connection between the servant and his Lord is called prayer. Furthermore, it is an expression of the fact that in Islam, the high and the low stand in the same rank; no one's head is raised above another's, and no one is ahead of another. This is the aspect of equality, and for this reason, after prayer, zakat is generally mentioned. Here, however, before zakat, ﴿and their affairs are by mutual consultation﴾ (42:38) is mentioned, so that it may be known that everyone's opinion is counted equally.

﴿And their affairs are by mutual consultation﴾ (42:38). The manner of expression is such that all their affairs are the result of consultation; as it were, their entire life is coloured by the hue of consultation. As we have said, this is a Meccan verse, and this command predates even the establishment of an Islamic state. This colour is not, as it were, specific only to governmental affairs; rather, it is the general conduct of an Islamic society, even though the government had not yet been established at that time.

The truth is that the organisation of government in Islam is in fact the organised manifestation of the features of Islamic society, and the Islamic government is also included within the Islamic society. Therefore, the Islamic society runs the Islamic government along the same lines as it runs its general affairs.

For this reason, the process of consultation was ongoing in Islamic society from the very beginning, and the scope of this consultation was far wider than the government and governmental commands. This is in fact a quality of Islamic society, and among the distinguishing qualities of that community which Allah has raised up for the leadership of all humanity, and for leadership it is of very great importance.

As for what the form of shura should be, Islam did not create any iron mould for it. In the circumstances of every time and place, its different form can be prepared, so that this quality, namely the spirit of shura, may be prevalent in Islamic society and also current in Islamic institutions. But it should have no rigid form; rather, the spirit of shura should be present everywhere. That is, this shura is in fact not the name of words and forms, but a quality which, as a result of faith, produces a consultative consciousness and conduct in Islamic society. Some people speak of Islamic institutions in which there is no faith at the core, or in which faith is not deemed necessary; they are doing a futile thing. And this is not a superficial matter, as it will appear at first sight, and especially it will appear to those who have not understood the importance of faith in the Islamic worldview. Because before the Islamic worldview is transferred into institutions and organisations, it contains within it intellectual and psychological realities which affect human thought and the human self. Afterwards these appear in the collective institutions of Islam as principles, taking a followed form, and then the texts come, and they point towards these forms and circumstances. The texts organise these principles; they do not create them, for their creation has already taken place through faith.

Therefore, for the manifestation of any form of the Islamic worldview, the existence of an Islamic society and of Muslims in a country is necessary, and those Muslims' faith must be active and effective. If Muslims do not exist at all, then merely by establishing institutions nothing is achieved. Mere institutions will not fulfil needs, and in that case no system will come into being that could be called Islamic.

When Muslims are truly present and faith comes into being in its reality, then the Islamic system will come into being by itself, and its institutional form will come into being automatically, which will be the need of those Muslims and the need of their society, and only in this way can the true fulfilment of the dream of Islamic principles come into being.

﴿And from what We have provided them, they spend﴾ (42:38). This verse also relates to the period before the command making zakat obligatory. Zakat became obligatory in the second year after the Hijrah, but spending in the way of Allah was a general command for the Islamic community even earlier. Indeed, this command came into existence together with the formation of the Islamic society.

The work of Islamic da'wah requires wealth, and this wealth will be obtained through spending. Through spending, the hearts of people are purified from the bad trait of miserliness, when the human urge for wealth comes under control and one learns to rely upon Allah rather than upon one's possessions. All these matters are necessary for the refinement of the meaning of faith. And it is clear that no collective system can be established without spending, because da'wah is a struggle, and in struggle the maintenance of workers is necessary so that collective needs may be met and results may be produced. At times this mutual support becomes so comprehensive that individuals are not even permitted to keep private wealth. When the Muhajirun left Makkah and, together with the Ansar in Madinah, a system was established, all of this was under this principle. But when conditions returned to normal, then zakat was put into practice and the system of mu'akhah (brotherhood), which was complete mutual support, was abrogated. In any case, spending in the way of Allah is the distinguishing feature of the community chosen for this purpose, or the community established for this purpose, that it should bring about an Islamic revolution in some region.

﴿And those who, when oppression afflicts them, they defend themselves﴾ (42:39). The mention of this quality in the Meccan surahs carries a special meaning within itself, as we said earlier. Through it, the intention is to show that within the Islamic community, the Muslim ummah has this natural quality, that they confront oppression. Confronting evil is an important duty, because if someone lays down his arms before an oppressor, the oppressor becomes more arrogant and bold. Therefore, confronting the oppressor is very necessary. And for a nation that was raised up precisely so that it would guard people's rights, with enjoining good as its mission and forbidding evil as its obligation, confronting evil is extremely important, because the ideal and goal of the Muslim ummah and the Muslim community is to dominate human life and to establish justice and fairness within it in truth.

﴿And honour belongs to Allah, to His Messenger and to the believers﴾. Therefore, the temperament of the Islamic community and the nature of its duties require that it confront oppression and defend itself against the acts of aggression being carried out against it. In Makkah the command was: hold back, restrain your hands and be patient; pray and give zakat. There, these commands were due to the specific circumstances of Makkah, and some training of the early Arab Muslims was also desired, because the Arabs were by temperament vengeful. These were not permanent commands for the Islamic community and Islamic society. In Makkah, for certain special reasons, the command was given that at any cost, peace and security for coexistence should not be allowed to slip away.

1. Because the harshness and oppression against the Muslims did not come from any organised government institution ruling the community of that time, since the political situation of the Arabian Peninsula was of an unorganised tribal nature. There, the persecution of Muslims was carried out, if a Muslim was a member of a tribe, by the tribe, and within the tribe no one but his close relatives would dare to do so. Muslims were not subjected to persecution as a community. Sometimes masters would persecute their Muslim slaves, and Muslims would buy them and set them free. Therefore no one dared to persecute their slaves excessively. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) did not wish that fighting should break out house by house in Makkah, with members of the same household who had become Muslim beginning to fight against non-Muslims. Moreover, in Makkah, gentleness softened the hearts of other people far more than harshness did.

Furthermore, Arab society was a society of self-respect and chivalry. In it, people would rise up in support of the oppressed. When Muslims endured suffering and remained firm upon their belief, the feelings of Arab chivalry would rise on their behalf. During the siege in Shi'b Abi Talib, it was generally that same feeling which helped the Muslims, in which all of Banu Hashim had been besieged. Against this blockade, people's sympathies turned in favour of the Muslims, and people tore to pieces the agreement that was in the document, and thus this unjust pact came to an end.

Moreover, it was the custom among the Arabs to draw the sword at the slightest matter. They were highly emotional and not bound by any discipline or order. The organisation desired in the Islamic community required that this emotionalism be restrained somewhat and be bound to a goal, and that people be made accustomed to nervous self-control and patience, and that a consciousness be created among people that ideology and ultimate aim take precedence over every emotion and every interest. Therefore, in Makkah, the continual exhortation to patience was very necessary for the methodology of Islamic training. In this way, the desired balance came into being in the personality of a Muslim, and they continued to advance with patience and steadfastness towards their goal.... In short, these and other similar reasons are known to Allah and His Messenger. Because of them, in Makkah, the exhortation to patience continued, but the real aim of the Islamic movement was always this.

﴿And those who, when oppression afflicts them, they defend themselves﴾ (42:39).

This principle is practically given effect by another principle of life, namely:

﴿And the recompense for an evil is an evil like it﴾ (42:40). The principle of punishment is that the penalty should be of the same kind as the crime, so that a person does not become rebellious. If a rebellious person has no one to restrain him, then he advances very comfortably in rebellion and oppression.

This is the right to redress of the wronged and the general principle. However, if someone pardons for the sake of reforming his own self, or for the sake of good recompense and reward in the Hereafter, or pardons due to feelings that arise against the Muslim community, then there is an exception to this rule. But forgiveness is considered meaningful only when a person has the power to answer evil with evil. At that time, the pardon carries weight, and the wrongdoer is also reformed, because when the aggressor thinks that the pardon and forgiveness were given purely out of generosity, and that there is no weakness on the part of the one who forgave, then he will feel ashamed, will become remorseful, and will refrain from such conduct in future. And he will think that my opponent has treated me with nobility; he is a high-minded person. And the one who has the ability to take revenge and yet forgives, his heart also becomes pure, because in such circumstances forgiveness and pardon are beneficial for both parties. But if a person is unable to take revenge and forgives, then the situation is: "The beggar's humility is his nature." Therefore, such pardon should not even be called pardon, because there is no pardon there; it is compulsion. And this situation is a mischief-producing situation. As a result, the oppressor becomes more emboldened, and corruption spreads. Consider this verse:

﴿فَمَنْ عَفَا وَأَصْلَحَ فَأَجْرُهُ عَلَى اللَّهِ﴾ (42:40) "So whoever pardons and makes reconciliation, his reward is with Allah."

﴿إِنَّهُ لَا يُحِبُّ الظَّالِمِينَ﴾ (42:40) "Indeed, He does not love wrongdoers."

This is an emphasis on the earlier principle that "the recompense for an evil is an evil like it." The meaning is: either forgive, or if you wish to take retribution, take an equal retribution, and do not exceed the limit.

A second emphasis of the same principle:

﴿وَلَمَنِ انتَصَرَ بَعْدَ ظُلْمِهِ فَأُولَٰئِكَ مَا عَلَيْهِم مِّن سَبِيلٍ﴾ (42:41) ﴿إِنَّمَا السَّبِيلُ عَلَى الَّذِينَ يَظْلِمُونَ النَّاسَ وَيَبْغُونَ فِي الْأَرْضِ بِغَيْرِ الْحَقِّ ۚ أُولَٰئِكَ لَهُمْ عَذَابٌ أَلِيمٌ﴾ (42:42) "And those who take retribution after being wronged, there is no blame upon them. The blame is only upon those who wrong people and transgress upon the earth without right; for them is a painful punishment."

Therefore, whoever defends himself after being wronged and takes an equal retribution for evil, without transgressing, there is no accountability upon him. He is exercising his lawful right. Therefore, no one has any argument against him, nor is it permissible for anyone to obstruct his path. The path should be blocked for those who oppress people and commit injustices on earth without entitlement, because no society can be reformed when an oppressor is oppressing people and there is no one to hold his hand. Where there is a rebel who is inflicting oppression upon people and there is no power to restrain him or to make him submit to retribution, Allah nevertheless threatens such oppressors with a painful punishment. But it is also the duty of the people to hold the oppressor's hand.

Finally, despite individual circumstances and the power of retaliation, attention is again drawn to balance, moderation, self-restraint, patience, and the attitude of goodness. When patience and goodness are truly a form of forgiveness, not humiliation, a genuine kindness, and not something one has been forced into:

﴿وَلَمَن صَبَرَ وَغَفَرَ إِنَّ ذَٰلِكَ لَمِنْ عَزْمِ الْأُمُورِ﴾ (42:43) "But whoever is patient and forgives, indeed that is of the matters requiring determination."

All the guidance and injunctions of this paragraph are based on great moderation and balance. Efforts have been made to protect the human self from grudge and anger on one side, and on the other side, to protect it from weakness, humiliation, and oppression and transgression. And in every condition, the pleasure of Allah is to be kept in view. And it has been explained that patience is, in every case, provision for the journey.

The qualities of the believers mentioned here are the characteristics of that revolutionary community which is to lead all of humanity, and whose aim is the reward of the Hereafter and the pleasure of God, and this is for those who believe and put their trust in their Lord.

After stating that these are the qualities of the believers and that the reward of the Hereafter for them is far better and everlasting, now, by way of contrast, the other side of the picture is presented: the end of some oppressors is also given here, and an announcement of humiliation and loss is made for them.

The passage opens by recalling that earlier in this surah the Qur'an described how the People of the Book (Ahl al-Kitab) differed among themselves after knowledge had come to them, and that these differences were not born of misunderstanding or ignorance. The clear Book of God had come to them, yet they divided out of envy and enmity. It was also stated that from the time of Noah, Abraham, Moses and Jesus (peace be upon them) God had established for people a heavenly religion (din samawi), a method (minhaj) and a system of life, and had enjoined them to establish it. It was further explained that those who, out of envy and enmity, differed regarding the divine method, and after them the later generations who received a Book, fell into doubt about the Books themselves because of these differences. If this was the condition of the People of the Book and the adherents of heavenly religion, then the condition of the nations that had no Book or religion at all must obviously be worse.

For this reason humanity needed righteous leadership that would bring people out of blind ignorance (jahiliyyah), guide them, and bind them together with a strong rope, directing them towards the path that leads to Allah, the Lord of this existence.

Therefore Allah sent down this final Book in the Arabic language to His last Prophet, Muhammad (ﷺ), so that he might begin the call among the people of Umm al-Qura, Makkah al-Mukarramah, and its surroundings, and establish among them the same religion that had been strictly enjoined upon Noah, Abraham, Moses and Jesus (peace be upon them). The purpose was that the links of all the true religions should join together, so that from the beginning of history until Muhammad (ﷺ) there would be one path, one method, one religion and one law. A community would be established here to safeguard this historic call, to lead it, and to bring this call into being on this earth in accordance with the will of Allah, and to establish this method here in the form that pleases Allah. Accordingly, in the verses under discussion, the features of the community that is to carry out this great obligation are being described.

It should be kept in view that these verses are Makkan and were revealed before the establishment of the Islamic system of government in Madinah. Yet even in Makkah we see one of the distinguishing characteristics of the Islamic movement (Tahrik-i Islami).

"Their affairs are conducted by mutual consultation" (42:38). This shows that the institution of consultation (shura) is an important part of Islamic society and of the life of the Muslims. It is a fundamental characteristic of the Islamic community. The organisation of the community is founded upon consultation, and this system then extends beyond the community to become part of the state. In other words, consultation is the life-blood of the Islamic society, and it spreads throughout it. In this way, the second characteristic of this community is described.

"Those who, when oppression afflicts them, defend themselves" (42:39). Although in Makkah the command had been: be patient, and do not repay evil with evil, and this command was in force until, after the Hijrah, permission for fighting (qital) was granted and it was said:

"Permission is given to those against whom war is being waged, because they have been wronged; and surely Allah is able to give them victory" (22:39).

The mention of this quality in these Makkan verses is therefore because it is the disposition of the Islamic movement to stand firm against oppression. The commands before and after this are for patience and restraint, while this is an exceptional ruling for a specific time. Since in this Makkan surah the fundamental qualities of the Muslim community were being recorded, it was mentioned here that although at present retaliation was prohibited, this quality is nonetheless among the fundamental qualities of the believers.

Nevertheless, to mention within the qualities of the Muslim community matters that were not being practised at that time, when the community did not hold practical leadership of any state and was still enduring hardships in Makkah, was done because this community was to lead all humanity and was established so that it would bring the whole of humanity out of darkness into the light of Islam. Therefore it was necessary that these qualities be developed within the community and that the community be prepared for these purposes. It is necessary to keep these matters in view so that when power comes into its hands it will be fit to wield it. Therefore these qualities require deep reflection: what are they, what is their reality, and what is their importance in human society?

These are the qualities of an Islamic community: faith (iman), reliance upon Allah (tawakkul), avoiding major sins (kaba'ir) and immoralities (fawahish), forgiveness at the time of anger, responding to the call of Allah, establishing prayer (iqamat al-salat), consultation in every matter, spending in the way of Allah (infaq fi sabil Allah), standing against oppression and transgression, pardon, reform, and patience. What are these, what is their reality, and what is their importance? It is appropriate to explain these qualities in the order in which the Qur'an presents them.

The Qur'an places people before the balance (mizan) established by Allah, which is firm and everlasting, so that they may distinguish between permanent and lasting values and temporary, changing circumstances. Their outlook must not be confused, otherwise the true worth of everything will not remain correct in their eyes. Therefore, before describing the qualities of the believers, Allah set out an enduring standard and measure, by which the qualities of a Muslim community are to be judged.

"Whatever you have been given is merely the enjoyment of the life of this world, and what is with Allah is better and more lasting" (42:36). The provisions of this earth are very alluring and dazzling: food and drink, children, desires, pleasures, status, authority and the like. Some blessings are those which Allah has given to His servants on the earth as an act of mercy, and these are pure bounty from Allah. Allah has not made them dependent in this world upon disobedience or obedience. Although a little bounty granted to an obedient person carries blessing, and even if an evildoer holds much, blessing is taken away from it.

But all these matters are not lasting values. They are a provision and the equipment of this life. This equipment is for a limited time. It neither elevates anyone's rank nor lowers it. It is not a proof of nobility and honour before Allah, nor a proof of disapproval and displeasure. It does not show that Allah is pleased with a person, nor does it show that Allah is angry with him. It is simply the provision of this life, this transient life, and in comparison with it:

"And what is with Allah is better and more lasting" (42:36). It is better in its worth, and more lasting because it is everlasting. Therefore the provisions of this transient world, in comparison with the Hereafter, are nothing. They are very limited and of little value, and they last only for a few days. For an individual they are useful only during his own life, and then each person should consider how much of his life he has brought with him and how much remains. And in comparison with the Days of Allah (ayyam Allah), this is very little, indeed like moments, as in the blink of an eye.

After this introductory statement and the explanation of the true criterion of good and evil, Allah now describes the qualities of those believers for whom He has prepared a better and more lasting end with Him.

"And what is with Allah is better and more lasting for those who believe" (42:36). Faith is a reality which, when it settles in the mind, makes it possible for human beings to determine the true "value" of everything in this universe. Only through faith can we grasp the reality of this universe, because the Lord of the worlds has told us about it. Only after grasping this reality can a person deal rightly with this universe. In this way a human being comes to know its reality, is able to understand the laws of nature within it, and can thereby bring his movement into harmony with the movement of this universe. Then a person will not deviate from the universal laws of nature, because such deviation would destroy this harmony, and this harmony is so important that with it a person can live a good life in this world, and together with that great existence can spend his life in obedience and submission to his Creator and Lord. This quality is necessary for every human being, that he be a believer; but the community which is to lead the journey of all humanity, and which is to bring all humanity to the Creator of the universe, must possess this quality to the highest degree.

What are the results of this faith? The believer attains psychological tranquillity and clarity of purpose. Doubt, bewilderment, fear and despair do not come near him, and these qualities are indispensable for ordinary life on this earth. But these qualities are essential for that community which is to guide other human beings along this difficult path.

Among the important values of faith is that the believer is free from base desires, personal aims, individual interests and the pursuit of gain. Only then will he be able to work for a lofty purpose. He will reflect that he has no personal share in this work; it is simply the duty of calling to Allah. He has already received his reward from Allah, and his bargain has been concluded with Allah. This awareness is especially necessary for the one who is the leader of the movement, so that he does not become despondent when a headstrong group separates from him or when he is harmed because of the call, and so that, if the whole public becomes his followers and obeys him, he does not become proud, for he is a labourer who has already taken his wages from Allah.

The truth is that the first group of Muslims, the community of the Companions, developed this kind of faith. Their faith brought about a remarkable revolution in their souls, their morals and their conduct. In their time the very form of faith had become distorted among all humanity. Faith had been suppressed; indeed, faith had no effect at all upon people's morals, conduct and psychology. When Islam came, it gave faith a living, effective and dynamic form, and it produced a group of Companions (may Allah be pleased with them) who took up the banner of the Islamic revolution.

* * *

Sayyid Abul Hasan Ali Nadwi, in his book "The Global Effects of the Decline of the Muslims" (Musalmanon ke Zawal ke Alami Asrat), says:

"This is the faith to which this verse alludes, and in it faith is mentioned as the first quality of the community raised up to lead all humanity, which, through its faith, leads humanity. The demand of this faith is that a believer relies upon Allah alone."

But the Qur'an mentions reliance upon Allah as a separate and independent theme:

"And upon their Lord they rely" (42:36). Here, instead of the ordinary phrase "yatawakkalna 'ala rabbihim", it says "wa 'ala rabbihim yatawakkalun" (42:36). By placing the prepositional phrase ahead of the verb, a sense of restriction (hasr) arises: they rely upon their Lord alone, and upon no one else. This too is the doctrine of Tawhid, and the first requirement of the doctrine of Tawhid is that they rely upon Allah. The believer has faith in the essence and attributes of Allah. He is certain that no person in this universe can do anything by his own will; nothing happens here without the permission of Allah. Therefore the believer relies upon Allah alone. In doing or not doing anything, the believer relies upon Allah alone.

This awareness is indispensable in the practical life of every person, because in this way he walks with his head held high before everyone, and his head does not bow before anyone. He will be very content; he will place no hope in anyone, and will have no fear of anyone. If difficulties come, he will be resolute and steadfast, and if times are good, he will remain sober. Neither prosperity nor adversity will be able to move him from his place. This awareness is very essential for the leader of the Islamic revolution, so that he may remain firm amid the ups and downs of this path, and this quality is also necessary for every member of the community that is bringing about the Islamic revolution.

"And who avoid the major sins and immoralities" (42:37). Purity of heart and a transparent conduct, especially avoidance of major sins and acts of immorality, is a fundamental characteristic of an Islamic society and is among the clear signs of faith. For a true leader, and especially for a community that rises to call to Islam, this is an extremely necessary quality. No heart can remain pure if it commits sins, participates in acts of immorality and does not avoid these things. No individual or community is fit for leadership if its heart is not clean, and if sin and immorality have themselves destroyed its faith and distorted its very form.

In the hearts of the first community of Muslims, faith had risen to such a degree and with such a keen sense of awareness that it is alluded to in the verse mentioned above (22), and in this way faith raised that community to the station of human leadership. They provided a leadership of a kind that is found neither in ancient history nor in modern history. Such leadership is like a sharp arrow that points to a star, in a world where the war of desires rages and there is a state of every man for himself.

Sayyid Qutb's commentary, Fi Zilal al-Quran (Urdu translation), on Surah 42, verses 36–43 (part 2 of 3):

Allah is well aware of the weaknesses of this human creation, so He has also kept the conditions of leadership within a reasonable limit, such that a leadership can act upon them and thereby obtain the reward that is stored with Allah. The standard that Allah has prescribed is that the Islamic community and its leadership should avoid major sins and indecencies. As for minor lapses, Allah will forgive them, because Allah is well aware of the limits and bounds of human obedience. This is the grace, kindness and mercy of Allah that He has shown to this human being. It is appropriate that we feel shame before Allah, because kindness creates feelings of modesty in a person, and forgiveness and pardon create honour and respect.

﴿And when they are angered, they forgive﴾ (42:37). This quality came immediately after a point had already been indicated: that Allah pardons the small sins of His servants and overlooks them. Therefore the servants too should treat one another with kindness and forgiveness. Accordingly, among the qualities of the believers it was included that when they become angry, they forgive one another.

In this matter too, Islam shows immense kindness to the human soul. Islam does not burden a person beyond his capacity. Allah knew that anger is a human reaction that arises from human nature, and that this anger is not purely evil. For the sake of Allah, for the sake of the religion of Allah, for the sake of truth and for the sake of justice, anger is desirable, and there is good in it. Therefore Islam does not declare the mere feeling of anger to be a crime, nor does it call it an error. Rather, Islam accepts anger as part of human temperament and nature. For this reason Islam does not create a separation or division between a person and his nature because of any religious command. Yes, Islam does guide that a person should control his anger. He should, as far as possible, act with pardon and forgiveness, and this will be an exemplary quality among his attributes of faith. In this regard, it is related about the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) that he never became angry over personal matters. His anger was for the sake of Allah, and then no force could withstand his anger. But this is the station and the perfection of the Muhammadan station (ﷺ). Allah commands ordinary Muslims only in accordance with their strength, although He tests them in this too, and He only commands that if anger comes, they should forgive, and if it is possible, they should pardon and control the feelings of vengeance, provided the matter is within personal bounds and is between two individuals.

﴿And those who respond to their Lord﴾ (42:38). They remove the obstacles that stand between them and their Lord, and they erase from the human soul whatever prevents attention toward Allah. These obstacles are the carnal desires, passions and inclinations, and those barriers that are attached to a person's being and self. When a person controls his personal desires and removes personal obstacles, then the path between him and his Lord becomes clear. Then he is ready at all times to carry out every command of his Lord, and no personal desire can become an obstacle before the command of Allah. This is the general quality of acting upon the commands of Allah, but some of the commands of Allah are also specifically mentioned here.

﴿And establish prayer﴾ (42:38). In Islam, prayer holds a very great station and rank. After the affirmation of the Kalimah Tayyibah, the first command that comes is that of prayer. As it were, prayer is the beginning of following the commands of Allah. The connection between the servant and his Lord is called prayer. Furthermore, it is an expression of the fact that in Islam, the high and the low stand in the same rank; no one's head is raised above another's, and no one is ahead of another. This is the aspect of equality, and for this reason, after prayer, zakat is generally mentioned. Here, however, before zakat, ﴿and their affairs are by mutual consultation﴾ (42:38) is mentioned, so that it may be known that everyone's opinion is counted equally.

﴿And their affairs are by mutual consultation﴾ (42:38). The manner of expression is such that all their affairs are the result of consultation; as it were, their entire life is coloured by the hue of consultation. As we have said, this is a Meccan verse, and this command predates even the establishment of an Islamic state. This colour is not, as it were, specific only to governmental affairs; rather, it is the general conduct of an Islamic society, even though the government had not yet been established at that time.

The truth is that the organisation of government in Islam is in fact the organised manifestation of the features of Islamic society, and the Islamic government is also included within the Islamic society. Therefore, the Islamic society runs the Islamic government along the same lines as it runs its general affairs.
